###### Article 761

The lessee cannot make any change to the land that diminishes its value.

If the lessee has made improvements or constructions that increase the value of the land, he cannot destroy them, nor claim any compensation in this regard.

###### Article 762

The lessee is liable for all contributions and charges on the property.

With regard to constructions existing at the time of the lease and those that will have been erected in performance of the agreement, he is liable for repairs of all kinds; but he is not obliged to rebuild the buildings if he proves that they were destroyed by fortuitous event, by force majeure, or that they perished due to a defect in the construction prior to the lease.

He is liable for fire, in accordance with Article 1394, paragraphs 2 and 3, of this code.

###### Article 763

The emphyteuta may acquire active servitudes for the benefit of the land, and burden it, by deed, with passive servitudes for a time that shall not exceed the duration of the lease and subject to notifying the owner.

###### Article 764

The emphyteuta benefits from the right of accession during the duration of the emphyteusis.

###### Article 765

In the event of expropriation for reasons of public utility, the lessor must make known the right of the emphyteuta, in accordance with the legal provisions in force. Separate compensation is granted to the lessor and to the lessee.

###### Article 766

The lessee alone has the hunting and fishing rights and exercises with regard to mines, mineral deposits, quarries and peat bogs all the rights of the usufructuary.

###### Article 767

The instrument creating the emphyteusis is subject only to the registration and transcription fees established for leases for a limited duration.
Transfers of any kind relating to either the right of the lessor or the right of the lessee are subject to the legal provisions concerning transfers of ownership of immovable property. The fee is assessed on the market value determined by an estimated declaration of the parties.

#### Chapitre V : Du droit de superficie Article 768

A land may be the subject of a division aimed at conferring on a third party the ownership of a part of that land situated above or below a conventionally fixed boundary. The ownership of the upper part is called superficiary ownership or right of superficies, that of the lower part subsoil ownership.

Thus, the right of superficies consists, for the holder of this right, in the fact of possessing constructions, works or plantations on land belonging to another.
For the holder of the right of ownership over the soil, the right of superficies is a waiver of accession.

The holder of the right of superficies may burden with servitudes the property that is the subject of his right, but only within the limit imposed for the exercise of that right.

###### Article 769

A land may also be the subject of a spatial division creating volumes. To each volume corresponds a full right of ownership.
A descriptive statement of division must obligatorily be executed by notarial deed.

### Titre IV : Des servitudes ou services fonciers

###### Article 770

A servitude is a charge that burdens a land for the use and utility of a land belonging to another owner.
It establishes neither pre-eminence of one land over the other nor personal obligations for the benefit or at the expense of the owners, but only relations between the servient land and the dominant land and the services attached to them.

It derives either from the natural situation of the places, or from obligations imposed by law, or from agreements between the owners.
Chapitre Ier : Des servitudes qui dérivent de la situation des lieux Article 771
Lower lands are subject towards those that are higher to receive the waters that flow naturally from them without the hand of man having contributed thereto.

The lower owner cannot raise a dike that prevents this flow.

The upper owner cannot do anything that aggravates the servitude of the lower land.

###### Article 772

Every owner has the right to use and dispose of rainwater that falls on his land.

If the use of this water or the direction given to it aggravates the natural servitude of flow established by Article 771, compensation is due to the owner of the lower land.
The same provision is applicable to spring waters arising on a land.

When, by borings or underground works, an owner causes waters to spring up in his land, the owners of the lower lands must receive them; but they are entitled to compensation in the event of damage resulting from their flow.

Houses, courtyards, gardens, parks and enclosures adjoining dwellings cannot be subjected to any aggravation of the servitude of flow in the cases provided for by the preceding paragraphs.
Disputes to which the establishment and exercise of the servitudes provided for by these paragraphs and the settlement, if necessary, of compensation due to the owners of the lower lands may give rise are brought, in first instance, before the judge of the district court of the canton who, in ruling, must reconcile the interests of agriculture and industry with the respect due to property.

If an expert assessment is necessary, only one expert may be appointed.

###### Article 773

He who has a spring in his land may always use the waters at his will within the limits and for the needs of his land.
The owner of a spring can no longer use it to the prejudice of the owners of the lower lands who, for more than thirty years, have made and completed, on the land where the spring gushes forth, apparent and permanent works intended to use the waters or to facilitate their passage into their property.
Nor can he use it in such a way as to deprive the inhabitants of a commune, village or hamlet of the water necessary to them; but if the inhabitants have not acquired or prescribed the use thereof, the owner may claim compensation, which is determined by experts.

If, from the exit of the land where they spring up, the spring waters form a watercourse offering the character of public and running waters, the owner cannot divert them from their natural course to the prejudice of the lower users.

###### Article 774

Every owner may compel his neighbor to mark the boundaries of their contiguous properties.

Boundary marking is the operation that makes it possible to recognize and fix, in a contradictory and definitive manner, the dividing boundaries of private properties belonging or intended to belong to different owners.
Boundary marking is carried out by mutual agreement of the parties and, failing that, by a decision of the judge seized by one of them or, within the framework of the registration procedure for the immovable property, by the sworn surveyor of the Cadastre section who has been designated by the Registrar to proceed with the boundary marking of the immovable property to be registered.

Boundary marking is done at common expense.

###### Article 775

The action for boundary marking is perpetual

###### Article 776

Every owner may enclose his land, subject to the exception relating to the right of passage set forth in Articles 794 and following.

#### Chapter II: Servitudes Established by Law Article 777

Servitudes established by law are governed by the rules that institute them.

##### Section I: Party Walls Article 778

A party wall is an undivided property right in a wall, fence or ditch.

###### Article 779

A wall, fence or ditch may only be constructed straddling the boundary line between two adjoining properties with the mutual agreement of the owners of said properties.
The one of the two who has not consented to this construction may not, in urbanized areas of the country, demand the demolition of the wall. He acquires by operation of law and free of charge the party wall rights therein.

###### Article 780

Existing walls, fences or ditches, constructed on the boundary line or on the line separating two properties, are presumed to be party walls, unless there is evidence to the contrary in title or fact.

###### Article 781

Unless there is evidence to the contrary in title:
-	a wall is deemed to belong solely to the owner of the property towards which its top is inclined in its entirety or on whose side there are architectural elements attesting to the original intention of the builders of the wall;
-	a ditch is deemed to belong solely to the owner of the property on whose side the earth deposit is located;
-	a fence is deemed to belong solely to the owner of the enclosed property if only one of the properties is enclosed.

###### Article 782

The costs of repair and reconstruction of a party wall, fence or ditch are divided between the owners in proportion to the rights of each, unless the costs were made necessary by the act of one of them. The latter must then bear the entire cost.
However, any owner of a party wall, fence or ditch may avoid these costs by abandoning his party wall rights, unless the wall supports a building belonging to him or the ditch serves to drain water from his property.

###### Article 783

Each of the owners may support his construction on the party wall.

###### Article 784

Any co-owner may raise the height of the party wall; but he must pay alone the cost related both to the raising and to future maintenance repairs above the current height of the common fence.

If the party wall is not in a condition to support the raising, the one who nevertheless intends to raise it must have the wall entirely rebuilt at his own expense, and any excess thickness that may be necessary must be taken from his side.
The neighbor who has not contributed to the raising may acquire party wall rights therein by paying half of the cost it incurred and the value of half of the land provided for the excess thickness, if there is
any. The cost that the raising incurred is estimated at the date of acquisition, taking into account the condition in which the raised part of the wall is found.

###### Article 785

Any owner adjoining a wall has the option to make it a party wall in whole or in part, by reimbursing to the owner of the wall half of the current value of the wall and half of the value of the land supporting the wall or the part of the wall.

This option does not apply to other types of fences or to ditches.

###### Article 786

No owner may carry out work affecting or potentially affecting the structure of the party wall, fence or ditch without the consent of the other or, failing that, the authorization of the judge.

###### Article 787

The fruits and products of a party hedge belong to the owners in equal shares.

The co-owner of a party hedge may destroy it up to the limit of his property, provided he constructs a wall on that limit. The same rule applies to the co-owner of a party ditch that serves only as a fence.

Trees located in the party hedge are party property like the hedge. Each owner may require the uprooting or pruning of a party tree as soon as it is isolated and does not form part of the fence.

##### Section II: Distances to Be Observed Between Neighboring Properties Article 788

Anyone who builds on his property is obliged to observe the distance prescribed by particular regulations and customs according to the works in question.

###### Article 789

Likewise, the planting of vegetation is governed by administrative regulations or by constant and recognized customs. In the absence thereof and subject to particular provisions on urban planning, it is only permitted to have trees, shrubs and bushes near the boundary of the neighboring property at a distance of two meters from the boundary line between the two properties for plantings whose height exceeds two meters, and at a distance of half a meter for other plantings.

###### Article 790

The neighbor may require that trees, shrubs and bushes planted at a lesser distance or whose branches extend over his property be uprooted or reduced to the legal height or distance. He may also cut himself what extends over his property, provided that this does not cause the withering of the plant in question, failing which he will be liable.
If it is the roots, brambles or twigs that extend over his property, he has the right to cut them himself at the boundary line. This right is imprescriptible.

The fruits that fall naturally from these branches belong to him.

###### Article 791

Openings are apertures or arrangements that allow a view towards the neighbor's property, such as a window, balcony or platform.
Lights are apertures or arrangements that allow air or light to pass through, but do not allow a view towards the neighbor's property, such as a translucent brick.
Openings and lights constitute external arrangements within the meaning of the provisions relating to servitudes. Consequently:
-	no aperture, neither opening nor light, is authorized when the wall is a party wall, unless all owners agree;
-	only openings are authorized when the wall is private and is established on the boundary line of the neighboring property;
-	when the wall is built by the owner of a property at a distance from the boundary between properties, any direct view must be 1.90 meters from that boundary; and any oblique view must be 0.60 meters from that same boundary. This distance is calculated from the center of the aperture to the boundary line between the properties.

###### Article 792

The distance rules provided for in the preceding article do not apply to apertures that open onto a space within the public domain, nor when particular provisions on urban planning provide for other rules.
They also do not apply when the contemplated aperture opens onto a property burdened with a servitude preventing construction, such as a right of way servitude, established in favor of the one who wishes to open the view, provided that the distance between the contemplated aperture and the limit of exercise of the servitude in the neighboring property is located at least three meters away.

##### Section III: Roof Drainage Article 793

Every owner must construct his roofs so that rainwater flows onto his property or onto the public road; he may not cause it to flow onto his neighbor's property.

##### Section IV: Right of Way Article 794

The owner whose properties are landlocked may claim a sufficient right of way over the properties of his neighbors, subject to compensation proportionate to the damage he may cause, unless the state of being landlocked was voluntarily created.
A property is landlocked if it has no access to the public road, or only insufficient access, to allow its normal use or agricultural, industrial or commercial exploitation.

###### Article 795

The right of way must normally be taken from the side where the route is shortest from the landlocked property to the public road, unless another route is less damaging in which case that route must be preferred.

###### Article 796

If the enclosure results from the division of a property following a sale, an exchange, a partition or any other contract, the right of way may only be claimed over the land that was the subject of such acts.

However, in the case where a sufficient passage could not be established over the divided properties, Article 794 would be applicable.

###### Article 797

The action for compensation, in the case provided for by Article 794, is subject to prescription, and the passage may be continued, even though the action for compensation is no longer admissible.
The maintenance of the passage is the responsibility of the owner of the dominant land, unless otherwise agreed.

###### Article 798

In case of cessation of the enclosure and regardless of the manner in which the location and mode of the servitude were determined, the owner of the servient land may, at any time, invoke the extinction of the servitude.
In the absence of an amicable agreement, this disappearance is established by a court decision.

#### Chapitre III: Servitudes established by act of man

##### Section I

Various types of servitudes that may be established on property Article 799
Servitudes are either continuous or discontinuous.

Continuous servitudes are those whose use is or can be continual without requiring the actual act of man: such are water conduits, drains, views and others of this kind.
Discontinuous servitudes are those that require the actual act of man to be exercised: such are rights of passage, drawing water, pasturage and other similar rights.

###### Article 800

Servitudes are apparent or non-apparent.

Apparent servitudes are those that are indicated by external works, such as a door, a window, an aqueduct.
Non-apparent servitudes are those that have no external sign of their existence, such as, for example, the prohibition to build on a property, or to build only to a determined height.

##### Section II: How servitudes are established Article 801

Servitudes that do not result from the configuration of the land or that are imposed by law can only be acquired by title.
By exception, continuous and apparent servitudes may be established by destination of the father of the family:

There is destination of the father of the family when, in the absence of a stipulation to the contrary in the act of division, it is proven that the two properties currently divided belonged to the same owner, and that the external works or improvements from which the servitude results were carried out by him before the division of the property and maintained since.

###### Article 802

If the owner of two properties between which there exists an apparent sign of servitude, disposes of one of the properties without the contract containing any agreement relating to the servitude, it continues to exist actively or passively in favour of the alienated property or on the alienated property.

###### Article 803

When a servitude is established, everything necessary to use it is deemed to be granted.

Thus the servitude of drawing water from another's fountain necessarily includes the right of passage.

##### Section III

Rights of the owner of the land to which the servitude is due Article 804
The person to whom a servitude is due has the right to carry out all works necessary to use it and to preserve it.

###### Article 805

These works are at his expense, and not at the expense of the owner of the servient land, unless the title establishing the servitude provides otherwise.

###### Article 806

Even in the case where the owner of the servient land is charged by the title to carry out at his expense the works necessary for the use or preservation of the servitude, he may always free himself from the charge by abandoning the servient land to the owner of the land to which the servitude is due.

###### Article 807

If the land for which the servitude was established comes to be divided, the servitude remains due for each portion, without however the condition of the servient land being aggravated.
Thus, for example, if it concerns a right of passage, all the co-owners shall be obliged to exercise it by the same place.

###### Article 808

The owner of the land subject to the servitude may not do anything that tends to diminish its use, or to make it more inconvenient.
Thus, he may not change the state of the premises, nor transfer the exercise of the servitude to a place different from that where it was originally assigned.

But however, if this original assignment had become more onerous to the owner of the servient land, or if it prevented him from making advantageous repairs thereto, he could offer to the owner of the other land a place equally convenient for the exercise of his rights, and the latter could not refuse it.

###### Article 809

For his part, the person who has a right of servitude may only use it according to his title, without being able to make, either in the land that owes the servitude, or in the land to which it is due, any change that aggravates the condition of the former.

##### Section IV: How servitudes are extinguished Article 810

Servitudes cease when things are in such a state that they can no longer be used.

They revive if things are restored in such a manner that they can be used.

###### Article 811

Any servitude is extinguished when the land to which it is due, and the land that owes it, are united in the same hand.

###### Article 812

The servitude is extinguished by non-use for thirty years, unless it is registered in the Land Register.

The period begins to run from the day on which the holder of the dominant land ceased to enjoy it, in the case of discontinuous servitudes, and from the day on which an act contrary to the servitude was done, in the case of continuous servitudes.

###### Article 813

If the land in favour of which the servitude is established belongs to several persons jointly, the enjoyment by one prevents extinctive prescription with regard to all.
If, among the co-owners, there is one against whom prescription could not run, such as a minor, he shall have preserved the right of all the others.

## LIVRE III. THE DIFFERENT WAYS IN WHICH PROPERTY IS ACQUIRED

General provisions

###### Article 814

Ownership of property is acquired and transferred by succession, by inter vivos or testamentary donation, by the effect of obligations, by accession or incorporation, by occupation, by tradition, by prescription, or any other mode of acquisition provided by law.

Titre Ier: Successions
Chapitre Ier: Opening of successions and seisin of heirs Article 815
Successions open, upon death, at the last domicile of the deceased.

They are devolved, when the deceased has not disposed of his property by gifts or will, according to the present provisions of the civil code whenever the spouses have opted for the civil code regime at the time of their marriage or when an unmarried person has expressed his or her wish to the civil registrar. Gifts and wills are authorized to the extent compatible with the hereditary reserve.

The provisions of this title apply to the succession of a person subject to bankruptcy proceedings, subject to the special provisions provided for in this area.

###### Article 816

Agreements that have the purpose of creating rights or renouncing rights over all or part of a succession not yet opened or of a property dependent thereon only produce effect in cases where they are authorized by law.

###### Article 817

The law regulates the order of succession among the different heirs and the surviving spouse.

Universal legatees and donees are seised under the conditions provided for in Title II, Inter vivos donations and wills, of this book.
In their absence, the succession is acquired by the State.

###### Article 818

Heirs and the surviving spouse are vested by operation of law with the property, rights and actions of the deceased, subject to the obligation to discharge all the charges of the succession.
The State must be sent into possession.

###### Article 819

The provisions of this title, in particular those concerning indivision and partition, apply as appropriate to universal legatees and legatees by universal title, or to donees by universal title, when not derogated from by a particular rule.

#### Chapter II

Qualifications required to inherit - Proof of the status of heir

##### Section I: Qualifications required to inherit Article 820

To inherit, it is necessary to exist at the moment of the opening of the succession or, having already been conceived, to be born viable.
A person whose absence is presumed within the meaning of articles 142 et seq. may inherit.

###### Article 821

Where several persons who had a vocation to inherit from one another perish in the same event, the order of deaths is established by all means.
Persons who die without it being possible to establish which survived the other are deemed to have died at the same instant, if at least one of them is called to the succession of the other.
The succession of each of them is then devolved to the persons who would have been called to receive it in their default.

###### Article 822

The following are unworthy to inherit, and, as such, excluded from successions:
1° A person who is convicted of having, alone or with others, voluntarily caused or attempted to cause the death of the deceased;
2° A person who is convicted of having, alone or with others, voluntarily inflicted blows or violence resulting in the death of the deceased, without intention to cause it;
3° A person who is convicted of having voluntarily refrained from preventing the commission of an offence against the bodily integrity of the deceased from which death resulted, when he could have done so without risk to himself or to third parties;
4° A person who, in criminal proceedings, brought against the deceased an accusation or testimony found to be false or defamatory;

5° An heir of full age who, having knowledge of the murder of the deceased, did not report it to the authorities. However, failure to report may not be invoked against ascendants and descendants of the murderer, nor against his relatives in the same degree, nor against his spouse, nor against his brothers or sisters, nor against his uncles and aunts, nor against nephews and nieces.

###### Article 823

Where, by reason of their death, criminal proceedings could not be pursued to their conclusion against persons who committed the acts mentioned in 1° and 2°, those persons may nevertheless be declared unworthy by the court on application by any heir and, failing that, by the public prosecutor. The application must be made within six months of the death.

###### Article 824

Where the deceased, subsequent to the facts constituting the cause of unworthiness, had knowledge thereof and expressly stated, in testamentary form, that he intended to maintain the heir in his rights or made him a universal or universal title liberality, that successor affected by a cause of unworthiness is not excluded from the succession.

###### Article 825

The heir excluded from the succession on grounds of unworthiness is bound to return all fruits and all revenues of which he has had enjoyment since the opening of the succession.

###### Article 826

The children of the unworthy person are not excluded by the fault of their author, whether they come to the succession in their own right, or by the effect of representation; but the unworthy person may not, in any case, claim, over the property of that succession, the usufruct which the law grants to fathers and mothers over the property of their children.

##### Section II: Proof of the status of heir Article 827

Proof of the status of heir is established by all means.
This does not derogate from practices concerning the issuance of certificates of ownership or inheritance by judicial or administrative authorities.

###### Article 828

Proof of the status of heir may result from a certificate of notoriety drawn up by a notary, at the request of one or more beneficiaries.
The certificate of notoriety must refer to the death certificate of the person whose succession is open and mention the supporting documents that could be produced, such as civil status certificates and, where applicable, documents concerning the existence of liberalities mortis causa that may have an impact on succession devolution.

It contains the affirmation, signed by the beneficiary or beneficiaries who are the authors of the request, that they have a vocation, alone or with others whom they designate, to receive all or part of the succession of the deceased.

Any person whose statements would appear useful may be called to the act.
Mention is made of the existence of the certificate of notoriety in the margin of the death certificate.

###### Article 829

The certificate of notoriety thus established is evidence until proof to the contrary.

A person who relies on it is presumed to have hereditary rights in the proportion indicated therein, and the heirs designated in the certificate of notoriety or their common agent are deemed, with respect to third parties holding property of the succession, to have free disposal of such property and, in the case of funds, free disposal thereof in the proportion indicated in the act.
The certificate of notoriety does not, in itself, constitute acceptance of the succession.

###### Article 830

A person who, knowingly and in bad faith, relies on an inaccurate certificate of notoriety incurs the sanctions provided for in article 888, without prejudice to damages.

#### Chapter III: Order of successions Article 831

Successions are devolved to the relatives and to the successor spouse of the deceased, in the order and according to the rules determined hereinafter.
A successor spouse is the surviving spouse who is not divorced.

##### Section I: Rights of relatives in the absence of a successor spouse

###### § 1. General provisions Article 832

The law does not distinguish according to the modes of establishment of filiation in regulating succession.

The rights resulting from adoptive filiation are regulated in Title IX of this code, relating to adoption under the Civil Code.

###### Article 833

In the absence of a successor spouse, relatives are called to inherit as follows: 1° Children and their descendants;
2° Father and mother; brothers and sisters and the descendants of the latter; 3° Ascendants other than father and mother;
4° Collaterals other than brothers and sisters and the descendants of the latter. Each of these four categories constitutes an order of heirs which excludes those following.

###### Article 834

Children or their descendants succeed to their father and mother or other ascendants, without distinction of sex or primogeniture, even if they are issue of different unions.

###### Article 835

Where the deceased leaves neither issue, nor brother, nor sister, nor descendants of the latter, his father and mother succeed him, each for one half.

###### Article 836

Where the father and mother died before the deceased and the latter leaves no issue, the brothers and sisters of the deceased or their descendants succeed him, to the exclusion of other relatives, ascendants or collaterals.

###### Article 837

Where the father and mother survive the deceased and the latter has no issue, but has brothers and sisters or descendants of the latter, the succession is devolved, for one quarter, to each of the father and mother and, for the remaining half, to the brothers and sisters or to their descendants.

Where only one of the father and mother survives, the succession is devolved for one quarter to that person and for three quarters to the brothers and sisters or to their descendants.

###### Article 838

When only the father or mother survives and the deceased has neither issue nor brothers or sisters nor descendants of the latter, but leaves one or more ascendants of the other branch than that of his or her surviving father or mother, the succession devolves one half to the father or mother and one half to the ascendants of the other branch.

###### Article 839

When the father and mother or one of them survive the deceased and the latter has no issue, they may in all cases exercise a right of return, up to the shares fixed in the first paragraph of Article 837, over property that the deceased had received from them by gift.
The value of the portion of property subject to the right of return is credited primarily against the succession rights of the father and mother.

When the right of return cannot be exercised in kind, it is executed in value, within the limit of the succession assets.

###### Article 840

In the absence of heirs of the first two orders, the succession devolves to ascendants other than the father and mother.

###### Article 841

In the absence of heirs of the first three orders, the succession devolves to the collateral relatives of the deceased other than brothers and sisters and the descendants of the latter.

###### § 2. Des degrés et des branches Article 842

Proximity of relationship is established by the number of generations; each generation is called a degree.

###### Article 843

The sequence of degrees forms the line. The direct line is the sequence of degrees between persons who descend one from the other, and the collateral line is the sequence of degrees between persons who do not descend from one another but who descend from a common ancestor.
The direct line is distinguished into the direct descending line and the direct ascending line. The first is that which connects the head with those who descend from him; the second is that which connects a person with those from whom he descends.

###### Article 844

In the direct line, there are as many degrees as there are generations between the persons. Thus, the child is, in relation to the father and mother, in the first degree; the grandson or granddaughter in the second; and reciprocally from the father and mother in relation to the child and from the grandparents in relation to the grandson or granddaughter; and so on.
In the collateral line, degrees are counted by generation, from one of the relatives up to but not including the common ancestor, and from the latter to the other relative. Thus, brothers and sisters are in the

second degree; the uncle or aunt and the nephew or niece are in the third degree; first cousins in the fourth degree; and so on.

###### Article 845

In each order, the nearest heir excludes the more remote heir in degree. Where degrees are equal, heirs succeed in equal shares and per capita.
All subject to what will be said hereafter concerning division by branches and representation.

###### Article 846

Collateral relatives belonging to the order of heirs mentioned in 4° of Article 833 do not succeed beyond the sixth degree.

###### Article 847

Relationship is divided into two branches, according to whether it proceeds from the father or the mother.
When the succession devolves to ascendants, it is divided in half between those of the paternal branch and those of the maternal branch.

###### Article 848

In each branch succeeds, to the exclusion of all others, the ascendant who is in the nearest degree.
Ascendants in the same degree succeed per capita.

In the absence of an ascendant in one branch, the ascendants of the other branch take the entire succession.

###### Article 849

When the succession devolves to collaterals other than brothers and sisters or their descendants, it is divided in half between those of the paternal branch and those of the maternal branch.

###### Article 850

In each branch succeeds, to the exclusion of all others, the collateral who is in the nearest degree.
Collaterals in the same degree succeed per capita.
In the absence of a collateral in one branch, the collaterals of the other branch take the entire succession.

###### § 3. De la représentation Article 851

Representation is a legal fiction, the effect of which is to call the representatives to the succession, in the place, in the degree and in the rights of the person represented.

###### Article 852

Representation takes place indefinitely in the direct descending line.

It is admitted in all cases, whether the children of the deceased compete with the descendants of a predeceased child, or whether all the children of the deceased having died before him, the descendants of said children are among themselves in equal or unequal degrees.

###### Article 853

Representation does not take place in favour of ascendants; the nearest, in each of the two lines, always excludes the more remote.

###### Article 854

In the collateral line, representation is admitted in favour of the children and descendants of brothers or sisters of the deceased, whether they come to his succession concurrently with uncles or aunts, or whether all the brothers and sisters of the deceased having predeceased, the succession is devolved to their descendants in equal or unequal degrees.

###### Article 855

In all cases where representation is admitted, the partition is effected by root, as if the person represented were coming to the succession: if the same root has produced several branches, the subdivision is also made by root in each branch. Within a root or a subdivision of a root, the partition is made per capita.

###### Article 856

Living persons are not represented, but only those who are dead; one may represent a person whose succession one has renounced.
Renouncing persons are represented only in successions devolved in the direct or collateral line.
The children of the renouncing person conceived before the opening of the succession from which the renouncing person was excluded bring back to the succession of the latter the property they inherited in his stead, if they come in competition with other children conceived after the opening of the succession. The bringing back is made according to the provisions set out in Articles 994 et seq. of this Code.

Unless the donor expresses a contrary intention, in case of representation of a renouncing person, gifts made to the latter are credited, where applicable, against the reserved portion that should have gone to him had he not renounced.

The law does not distinguish, for the exercise of representation, between legitimate filiation and natural filiation.

###### Article 857

Representation is admitted in favour of the children and descendants of the unworthy person, even though the latter is living at the opening of the succession.
The provisions set out in the second paragraph of Article 856 are applicable to the children of the unworthy person during his lifetime.

##### Section II : Des droits du conjoint survivant

###### § 1. De la nature des droits, de leur montant et de leur exercice Article 858

The successor spouse is called to the succession, either alone or in competition with the relatives of the deceased.

###### Article 859

If the predeceased spouse leaves children or descendants, the surviving spouse takes, at his or her choice, the usufruct of all the existing property or ownership of one quarter of the property when all the children are issue of both spouses and ownership of one quarter in the presence of one or more children who are not issue of both spouses.

###### Article 860

If, in the absence of children or descendants, the deceased leaves his father and mother, the surviving spouse takes one half of the property. The other half devolves one quarter to the father and one quarter to the mother.

When the father or mother has predeceased, the share that would have gone to him or her passes to the surviving spouse.

###### Article 861

In the absence of children or descendants of the deceased and of his father and mother, the surviving spouse takes the entire succession.

###### Article 862

By way of derogation from Article 861, in the event of the predeceasing of the father and mother, property that the deceased had received from his or her ascendants by succession or donation and which is found in kind in the estate is, in the absence of descendants, devolved for one half to the brothers and sisters of the deceased or to their descendants, themselves descendants of the predeceased parent or parents from whom the transmission originated.

###### Article 863

When the surviving spouse receives all or three-quarters of the property, the ascendants of the deceased, other than the father and mother, who are in need benefit from a maintenance claim against the estate of the predeceased.
The time limit for claiming it is one year from the death or from the time when the heirs cease to provide the benefits they previously provided to the ascendants. The time limit is extended, in case of joint ownership, until the completion of the partition.
The pension is taken from the estate. It is borne by all heirs and, in case of insufficiency, by all particular legatees, in proportion to their emolument.

However, if the deceased expressly declared that a particular legacy shall be satisfied in preference to others, Article 1080 shall apply.

###### Article 864

When the spouse has the choice of ownership or usufruct, his or her rights are non-transferable as long as he or she has not exercised his or her option.

###### Article 865

The spouse's option between usufruct and ownership may be proved by any means.

Any heir may invite the spouse in writing to exercise his or her option. Failing to have taken a position in writing within three months, the spouse is deemed to have opted for usufruct.

The spouse is deemed to have opted for usufruct if he or she dies without having taken a position.

###### Article 866

The calculation of the right in full ownership of the spouse provided for in Articles 859 and 860 shall be made on a mass consisting of all property existing at the death of his or her spouse to which shall be notionally reunited that which he or she disposed of, either by act inter vivos or by testamentary act, in favour of successors, without dispensation from bringing into account.
The spouse may only exercise his or her right over property which the predeceased has not disposed of either by act inter vivos or by testamentary act, and without prejudice to the rights of reserve or to rights of return.

###### Article 867

Liberalities received from the deceased by the surviving spouse are imputed to the rights of the latter in the succession. When the liberalities thus received are less than the rights defined in Articles 859 and 860,

the surviving spouse may claim the balance, without ever receiving a portion of the property greater than the available portion defined in Article 1228.

###### § 2. On the conversion of usufruct Article 868

Any usufruct belonging to the spouse over the property of the predeceased, whether it results from law, a will or a donation of property to come, gives rise to a power of conversion into a life annuity, at the request of one of the bare-owner heirs or of the successor spouse himself or herself.

The power of conversion is not susceptible to waiver. Co-heirs cannot be deprived of it by the will of the predeceased.

###### Article 869

In the absence of agreement between the parties, the request for conversion is submitted to the judge. The request for conversion may be brought until the final partition.
If he grants the request for conversion, the judge determines the amount of the annuity, the security that the debtor co-heirs must provide, as well as the type of indexation appropriate to maintain the initial equivalence of the annuity to the usufruct.
However, the judge cannot order against the will of the spouse the conversion of the usufruct relating to the dwelling that he or she occupies as a principal residence, as well as the furniture furnishing it.

###### Article 870

By agreement between the heirs and the spouse, the spouse's usufruct may be converted into capital.

###### Article 871

The conversion of usufruct is included in the partition operations. It does not produce retroactive effect, unless otherwise stipulated by the parties.

###### § 3

On the right to temporary housing and the life right to housing Article 872
If, at the time of death, the successor spouse effectively occupies, as a principal residence, a dwelling belonging to the spouses or totally dependent on the estate, he or she has by operation of law, for one year, the free enjoyment of that dwelling, as well as of the furniture, included in the estate, that furnishes it.

If his or her housing was provided by means of a rental lease or a dwelling belonging in undivided part to the deceased, the rent or the occupancy indemnity shall be reimbursed to him or her by the estate during the year, as and when they are paid.
The rights provided for in this article are deemed direct effects of marriage and not succession rights. This article is a matter of public policy.

###### Article 873

In addition, unless otherwise intended by the deceased expressed in the conditions of Article 1127, the successor spouse who effectively occupied, at the time of death, as a principal residence, a dwelling belonging to the spouses or totally dependent on the estate, has over that dwelling and over the furniture included in the estate that furnishes it, until his or her death, a right of habitation and a right of use.

When the dwelling is the subject of a rental lease, the successor spouse, if he or she effectively occupied the premises as a principal residence at the time of death, benefits from the right of use over the furniture included in the estate furnishing it.
The deprivation of these rights of habitation and use expressed by the deceased in the conditions mentioned in the first paragraph is without effect on the usufruct rights that the spouse receives by virtue of law or a liberality, which continue to obey their own rules.

These rights of habitation and use are exercised in the conditions provided for in Articles 745 paragraph 3, 747 and 748.

The spouse, the other heirs or one of them may require that an inventory of the movables and a statement of the immovable subject to the rights of use and habitation be drawn up.
By way of derogation from Article 745, paragraph 3, when the situation of the spouse is such that the dwelling burdened with the right of habitation is no longer adapted to his or her needs, the spouse or his or her representative may lease it for use other than commercial or agricultural in order to generate the resources necessary for new accommodation conditions.

###### Article 874

The value of the rights of habitation and use is imputed to the value of the succession rights received by the spouse.
If the value of the rights of habitation and use is less than that of his or her succession rights, the spouse may take the balance from the existing property.

If the value of the rights of habitation and use is greater than that of his or her succession rights, the spouse is not required to compensate the estate for the excess.

###### Article 875

The spouse has one year from the death to express his or her will to benefit from these rights of habitation and use.
The successor spouse and the heirs may, by agreement, convert the rights of habitation and use into a life annuity or into capital.

If there is among the successors parties to the agreement a minor or a protected adult, the agreement must be authorized by the President of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance.

###### § 4. Du droit à pension Article 876

The estate of the predeceased spouse owes a pension to the surviving spouse who is in need. The time limit to claim it is one year from the death or from the moment when the heirs cease to provide the benefits they previously furnished to the spouse. The time limit is extended, in case of undivided ownership, until the completion of the partition.
The maintenance pension is taken from the estate. It is borne by all heirs and, in case of insufficiency, by all particular legatees, proportionally to their emolument.

However, if the deceased has expressly declared that a particular legacy shall be paid in preference to others, Article 1080 shall apply.

#### Chapitre IV. Des droits de l'Etat

###### Article 877

In the absence of heirs, surviving spouse, universal legatees or donees, the estate passes to the State.
The State is required to have seals affixed and, if the inventory of assets has not already been carried out within the framework of the procedure provided for unclaimed estates, the domain authority shall have it carried out in the forms prescribed for acceptance of estates under benefit of inventory.

###### Article 878

It must request the grant of possession from the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the estate is opened.
The State is exempted from using the services of a lawyer; the court rules on the application three months and forty days after publication and posting in the customary forms, and after having heard the public prosecutor.

###### Article 879

In the case where vacancy had been regularly declared, and the domain administration appointed as curator, it may, before filing its application, proceed by itself with the publicity formalities provided for.

###### Article 880

The domain administration that has not fulfilled the formalities prescribed to it may be ordered to pay damages to the heirs, if any come forward.

#### Chapitre V : De l'option de l'héritier

##### Section I : Dispositions générales Article 881

Every successor, the heir with regard to the estate as the legatee with regard to the legacy that falls to him, may:
-	either accept it purely and simply,
-	or accept it under benefit of inventory, when he has a universal or universal title vocation,
-	or renounce it.

###### Article 882

The option is indivisible. However, the successor who combines more than one succession vocation has, for each of them, a distinct right of option.

###### Article 883

This option cannot be exercised before the opening of the estate, nor by marriage contract nor with the consent of the person whose estate is at issue.
A conditional or term option is null and void.

###### Article 884

The heir of subsequent rank has the same rights as the heir when the latter renounces the estate or is struck by unworthiness, from the day he became aware of the renunciation or unworthiness. The same applies to the heirs of one who dies without having opted, from the death of his predecessor; these heirs of one who dies without having opted exercise the option separately, each for his share.

###### Article 885

The power to accept or renounce an estate is prescribed by ten years. At the end of this period, the successor is deemed to have renounced the estate. One who claims to have accepted this estate before the expiration of this period must provide proof thereof.

###### Article 886

The subsequent heir of an heir whose acceptance is annulled only sees the ten-year period run against him from the final decision finding this nullity.
The heir who has left the surviving spouse in enjoyment of the hereditary property only sees the period run against him from the death of the latter.

The period does not run either against one who, legitimately, was unaware of the birth of his right, in particular the opening of the estate.

Moreover, as long as the prescription of the right to accept is not acquired against the heirs who have renounced, they have the power to still accept the estate, if it has not already been accepted by other heirs; without prejudice nevertheless to the rights that may be acquired by third parties over the property of the estate.

###### Article 887

The option exercised has retroactive effect to the day of the opening of the estate.

However, error, fraud as well as duress are a cause of nullity of the option exercised by the heir. The action for nullity is prescribed by five years from the day on which the error or fraud was discovered or the day on which the duress ceased.

###### Article 888

The heir who, knowingly and in bad faith, has concealed property or rights of an estate, or concealed the existence of a co-heir, or omitted to include in the inventory property or rights of the estate, is deprived of the benefit of inventory and the right of renunciation: he is an unconditional heir, without prejudice to the damages that the victims of his actions could claim.
The heir cannot however claim any share in the property or rights misappropriated or concealed. Likewise, when the concealment related to a donation subject to collation or reduction, the heir owes the collation or reduction of this donation without being able to claim any share therein. The concealing heir is moreover required to return all fruits and revenues of the concealed property which he has enjoyed since the opening of the estate.

###### Article 889

The personal creditors of one who abstains from accepting an estate or who renounces an estate to the prejudice of their rights may be authorized in court to accept the estate on behalf of their debtor, in his place and stead.
The acceptance takes place only in favor of these creditors and up to the amount of their claims. It produces no other effect with regard to the heir.

###### Article 890

The acceptance of an estate that would be absorbed or diminished by more than half, by the discovery of a will unknown at the time of acceptance, is voidable for lesion.

##### Section II : De l'acceptation de la succession

###### Article 891

Estates that have fallen to minors and adults under guardianship may only be validly accepted in accordance with the provisions of the title On Minority, Guardianship and Emancipation.

###### Article 892

The acceptance of the estate may be express or tacit: it is express when the successor takes the title or quality of heir in an authentic or private act; it is tacit when the successor performs an act that necessarily presupposes his intention to accept and that he would only have the right to perform in his quality as heir.
Purely conservatory, supervisory and provisional administration acts are not, by themselves, acts constituting acceptance on the part of the heir. If the successor wishes to take another act without however taking the title or quality of heir, he must request authorization from the judge to perform it.

###### Article 893

The following are deemed purely conservatory:
1° The payment of funeral and last illness expenses, taxes owed by the deceased, rents and other estate debts whose settlement is urgent;
2° The collection of fruits and revenues of estate property or the sale of perishable property, subject to justifying that the funds have been used to extinguish the debts referred to in 1° or have been deposited with a notary or placed in escrow;
3° Any act intended to prevent the aggravation of the estate liabilities;
4° Acts related to the termination of the employment contract of the employee of the deceased private employer, the payment of wages and compensation owed to the employee as well as the delivery of end-of-contract documents.

###### Article 894

The following are deemed to be acts of provisional administration:
1° The renewal, whether as lessor or lessee, of leases which, in the absence thereof, would give rise to the payment of compensation;
2° The implementation of administrative or dispositive decisions initiated by the deceased and necessary for the proper functioning of the enterprise;
3° Acts which are routine operations necessary for the short-term continuation of the activity of the enterprise forming part of the succession.

###### Article 895

The heir who, whether gratuitously or for consideration, transfers his rights in the succession, either to a third party, or to all his co-heirs, or to some of them, accepts the succession by that fact alone.
The same applies when the heir has renounced the succession, gratuitously or not, in favour of one, several or all of his co-heirs, or in favour of one, several or all heirs of subsequent rank.

###### Article 896

Where a person to whom a succession has devolved has died before being able, expressly or tacitly, to express his choice, his heirs may accept it or renounce it on his behalf. In the absence of unanimity among them, the succession must be accepted subject to inventory.

###### Article 897

When the heir accepts the succession, the effect of the acceptance relates back to the day of the opening of the succession.

##### Section III: Renunciation of successions Article 898

Renunciation of a succession is not presumed. It is enforceable against all from the day on which it is made at the registry of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the succession opened, in a special register kept for that purpose.

###### Article 899

The heir who renounces is deemed never to have been an heir.

###### Article 900

The succession to which the heir renounces is distributed among his heirs in the direct line; in the absence of heirs in the direct line, it passes to the co-heirs and otherwise to the next degree.
The heir who renounces the succession may nevertheless retain the inter vivos gift or claim the legacy made to him up to the amount of the available portion, unless the disposer has expressly required contribution in the event of renunciation. In that case, contribution is made in value; where the value contributed exceeds the rights he should have had in the partition had he participated therein, the renouncing heir compensates the accepting heirs to the extent of that excess.

##### Section IV: Acceptance subject to inventory

###### § 1. Formalities to be observed Article 901

The declaration of an heir that he intends to take that capacity only subject to inventory must be made at the registry of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the succession opened. It must be recorded in the register intended to receive acts of renunciation.

###### Article 902

The declaration mentions the surnames, given names, occupation of the heir and the capacity by virtue of which he is called to the succession.
It also includes the election of a single domicile located in Djibouti, which may be the domicile of one of the acceptors subject to inventory or that of the person responsible for settling the succession. It is to this address that creditors shall declare their claims.

###### Article 903

The heir's declaration is registered by the registry, which gives him a receipt therefor, and opens a file. The receipt informs the declarant of the need to satisfy the publication requirement provided for by the following article.

###### Article 904

The declaration is published, within fifteen days, in a newspaper authorized to receive legal publications.
Where the law refers to the declaration as the starting point of a time limit, that time limit runs from the date of the publication made.

###### Article 905

The heir's declaration has effect only insofar as it is preceded or followed by a faithful and accurate inventory of the property of the succession and within the time limits to be determined hereinafter.

###### Article 906

The heir has, first, three months to make an inventory, from the day of the opening of the succession.

He may however apply to the judge for an additional time limit if he justifies serious and legitimate reasons which delay the filing of the inventory. In that case, the time limit is suspended from the date of the application for extension.

The heir has, next, forty days to deliberate on his acceptance or not of the succession. This second time limit begins to run from the day of expiration of the time limit to which the heir is subject to make the inventory, or from the day of closure of the inventory if it has been completed before the three months.

###### Article 907

The inventory is descriptive and estimative of the elements present, item by item, in the deceased's estate.
It is drawn up by a bailiff or a notary, according to the rules applicable to those professions.

###### Article 908

A copy of the inventory is delivered against receipt by the heir to the competent registry, which adds it to the file. The heir must carry out this formality within two months of the inventory being made. Failing this, he is deemed to accept the succession purely and simply.

###### Article 909

The inventory gives rise to the same publication as the initial declaration.
Any person who justifies his status as creditor against the deceased may take cognizance of its contents and obtain a copy thereof at the registry.

###### § 2. Effects of acceptance subject to inventory Article 910

The declaration made by the heir to accept the succession subject to inventory entails:
1° Separation of estates: the heir's personal property is not merged with that of the succession;
2° Preservation of all the rights which the heir previously had over the deceased's property; 3° Limitation of the acceptance of the succession to the succession assets: the heir is bound to pay the debts of the succession only within the limit of the assets collected and not from his personal estate. The heir may be held liable in respect of his acts on his personal property only where provisions of this paragraph so provide;
4° Supervision of the management of the succession assets by the heir, who is bound to administer the succession.

###### Article 911

During the period of the time limits for making an inventory and for deliberating, the heir cannot be compelled to exercise his option. No judgment can be obtained against him.
As long as the prescription of the right to accept has not been acquired against him, the heir may revoke his acceptance and accept the succession purely and simply. He is then deemed to have accepted it from the opening of the succession.

Acceptance subject to inventory precludes any renunciation of the succession.

###### Article 912

If the heir does not file the inventory within the time limits provided for making it, or does not exercise his option within the time limit offered for deliberating, he retains the power to make an inventory and to opt.

It is otherwise if he has in other respects performed an act manifesting his intention to accept the succession purely and simply or if there exists against him a judgment having acquired the force of res judicata which condemns him in the capacity of heir purely and simply.

###### Article 913

However, upon expiration of the time limits provided for making an inventory and for deliberating, the heir who has not made an option may be summoned, by extrajudicial act, to take a position. The summons may be issued by a creditor of the succession, a co-heir, an heir of subsequent rank, or the State.
Within two months following the summons, the heir must take a position or request an additional time limit from the judge when he has not been able to complete the inventory begun or when he justifies other serious and legitimate reasons. This time limit is suspended from the request for extension until the decision of the judge seized.

In the absence of having taken a position upon expiration of the two-month time limit or the additional time limit granted, the heir is deemed to have accepted unconditionally.

###### Article 914

From the publication of the declaration of the heir who accepts the succession subject to inventory, the creditors of the succession have a period of twelve months to claim what is owed to them. They must declare their claim within this time limit, by notifying their title to the elected domicile of the succession.
In case of late declaration or absence of declaration, claims not secured by security interests on the assets of the succession are extinguished with regard to the succession.

This provision also benefits sureties and co-obligors, as well as persons having granted an independent guarantee relating to the claim thus extinguished.

###### Article 915

From the publication of the declaration of acceptance subject to inventory and for a period of twelve months, it stops or prohibits any means of execution and any new registration of security interest by the creditors of the succession, relating to both movables and immovables.
However, seizing creditors are considered as holders of security interests on the assets and rights previously seized.

###### Article 916

When the succession has been accepted by one or more heirs unconditionally and by one or more others up to the net assets, the rules applicable to this latter option are binding on all heirs until the day of partition.
The creditors of a succession accepted by one or more heirs unconditionally and by others up to the net assets may provoke the partition as soon as they justify difficulties in the recovery of the share of their claim incumbent upon the heirs accepting up to the net assets.

###### Article 917

The heir accepting up to the net assets has the obligation to administer the assets he receives in the succession, and must account for his management.
He is liable for serious faults he would commit in this administration.

He must present the account to any succession creditor who requests it and respond within a time limit of two months to the summons, served by extrajudicial act, to reveal to him where the assets and

rights received in the succession that he has neither alienated nor retained are located. Failing this, he may be compelled on his personal assets.

If he does not wish to personally administer the assets of the succession, or if he is in default, a representative may be appointed by court at the request of any interested party. The President of the Court of First Instance is seized and rules by summary order.

###### Article 918

The heir is the owner of the assets of the succession and has the power to dispose of the assets of the succession.
If there are in the succession objects liable to perish or too costly to preserve, the heir may proceed with the sale of these objects. If the heir has decided to retain such assets in kind, at the end of the acceptance procedure subject to inventory, he is liable only for the depreciation or deterioration caused by his negligence.

###### Article 919

For other assets, within the time limit of twelve months from the publication provided for in Article 904, the heir may declare:
1° that he intends to retain in kind certain assets of the succession. He then owes to the succession the value of these assets as it was estimated in the inventory;
2° that he sells certain assets, movable or immovable.
These assets are excluded from the succession estate and withdrawn from the security of succession creditors. On the other hand, their value is recorded in the assets of the succession. All without prejudice to the rights of creditors holding security interests.
The other succession assets that have not been the subject of such a declaration remain in the security of the creditors of the succession.

###### Article 920

The declaration of the alienation or retention of one or more assets is made within fifteen days at the registry of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance. The heir ensures its publication in a newspaper authorized to receive legal publications.
Without prejudice to the rights reserved to creditors holding security interests, any succession creditor may contest before the judge, within a time limit of three months after the publication mentioned in the first paragraph, the value of the retained asset or, when the sale was made amicably, the price of the alienation by proving that the value of the asset is higher.

When the creditor's request is granted, the heir is liable for the supplement on his personal assets, except to restore to the succession the retained asset.
The creditor may also act in his own name to have declared unenforceable against him the acts done by his debtor in fraud of his rights, provided he establishes, if it concerns an act for valuable consideration, that the third party co-contractor had knowledge or should have had knowledge of the fraud.

###### Article 921

The declaration to retain an asset is not enforceable against creditors as long as it has not been published.

The failure to declare the alienation of an asset within the time limit provided for in the preceding article binds the heir on his personal assets up to the amount of the price of the alienation.

###### Article 922

The heir settles the liabilities of the succession. He draws up for this purpose a draft settlement of liabilities.

The costs of seals, if any have been affixed, of inventory and of account, are borne by the succession. The public officer or ministerial officer having settled the succession or enabled the preservation of succession assets shall be paid before the other creditors.
Registered creditors are paid according to the rank of the security interest securing their claim.

The other creditors who have declared their claim are satisfied in the order of declarations. Legacies of sums of money are delivered after payment of creditors.

###### Article 923

The draft settlement of liabilities is filed at the registry which adds it to the file. A notice is published according to the publication procedures provided for in Article 904. Creditors who are not fully satisfied in view of this draft may, within one month of the publication, seize the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance in order to contest the settlement draft.

###### Article 924

In the absence of contestation at the end of the one-month time limit from the publication provided for in the preceding article, the heir must pay the creditors within the two months that follow, in accordance with the draft settlement of liabilities.
When, conversely, the settlement draft is not validated due to a contestation relating to the order or nature of the claims, the heir deposits the available sums as long as the contestation subsists.

###### Article 925

The personal creditors of the heir may only pursue recovery of their claims against the assets of the estate after the expiry of a twelve-month period from the publication of the declaration of acceptance of the estate subject to inventory and after the full satisfaction of estate creditors and legatees.
Creditors who have not declared their claim within the period referred to in the preceding article, and who come forward only after the exhaustion of the assets, have recourse only against the legatees who have been satisfied in their rights.

##### Section V: Vacant Estates Article 926

An estate is vacant when, after the expiry of the periods for making an inventory and for deliberating: 1° No person comes forward claiming an estate and there is no known heir;
2° All known heirs have renounced the estate;
3° Known heirs have been summoned to take a position in accordance with the provisions of Article 913 and have renounced the estate or remained silent;
4° In the absence of a summons, known heirs have not opted, either expressly or tacitly, for ten years.
When heirs come forward during the proceedings, their hereditary prerogatives take precedence. They may then exercise their legal right of option: if they accept the estate unconditionally, the vacancy automatically ends; if they renounce it, it continues; and if they accept subject to inventory, the proceedings continue according to the rules set out in Section IV of this chapter.

###### Article 927

The President of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the estate is opened, appoints a curator upon the application of any interested person or upon the requisition of the Public Prosecutor.

His decision is, at the initiative of the curator, within fifteen days of its pronouncement, published in a newspaper authorized to receive legal notices.

In the context of vacant estates, the curatorship is necessarily entrusted to the administrative authority responsible for the domain.

###### Article 928

The curator is required, first of all, to have its condition established by an inventory: he exercises and pursues its rights; he responds to claims brought against the estate; he administers, under the obligation to have the sums of money found in the estate, as well as the amounts from the sale price of movables or immovables sold, paid into the National Treasury, for the preservation of rights and under the obligation to account to whom it may concern.
The provisions of Section IV of this chapter, on the forms of inventory, on the mode of administration and on the accounts to be rendered by the beneficiary heir, as well as on the rights and obligations of creditors, are common to curators of vacant estates, subject to the following reservations.

###### Article 929

Creditors must declare their claim to the curator, by notifying him of their title, within a period of nine months.
The curator establishes a draft settlement of liabilities respecting the order provided for in Article 922, with the costs related to the administration of the curatorship being paid before other claims. The curator may only provide for the payment of estate debts up to the amount of the assets.

The curator may however pay, without waiting for the draft settlement of liabilities, the costs necessary for the preservation of the estate, funeral and last illness expenses, taxes owed by the deceased, rents and other estate debts whose settlement is urgent.

###### Article 930

The draft settlement of liabilities is filed with the registry of the Court of First Instance which adds it to the file. A notice is published according to the publication procedures provided for in Article 904.

###### Article 931

Creditors who are not fully satisfied in view of this draft may, within one month of the publication, seize the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance to contest the settlement draft.
Those who have not declared their claim after the submission of the draft may only claim the remaining assets. In case of insufficiency of these assets, they have recourse only against the legatees who have been satisfied in their rights. This recourse is prescribed after one year from the realization of all the remaining assets.

###### Article 932

In the absence of recourse against the draft or after the president's decision has become final, the curator proceeds with the final realization of the remaining assets.
Any surplus is handed over upon their request to heirs who come forward, if they are within the useful period to claim the estate.

The Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the estate is opened, seized by the curator, sends the State into possession of the estate.

#### Chapter VI. Partition

##### Section I: Legal Regime of Joint Ownership

###### § 1. General Provisions Article 933

Joint ownership arises when several persons have a real right of the same nature over the same property or the same mass of property. This right may be ownership or another dismembered real right.
Joint ownership does not have legal personality.
Each co-owner has over the jointly owned property the same right shared with the others. The extent of each person's rights in the joint ownership is defined by the law or the agreement that gives rise to it. In the absence of another title, it results from a certificate of notoriety or an inventory heading established by the notary.

###### Article 934

Each co-owner holds his share. However, when a co-owner intends to transfer all or part of his undivided rights, for consideration and to a person outside the joint ownership, the other co-owners have a right of pre-emption.
Any transfer project must be notified beforehand to the other co-owners, with all useful information, such as the price, the conditions of the transfer and the identifying elements of the purchaser. This notification, made by extra-judicial act, opens a one-month period for the co-owners to bring to the knowledge of the transferring co-owner their decision to exercise their right of pre-emption under the conditions brought to their knowledge.
The person who decides to pre-empt has two months to complete the transfer, from the sending of his decision to the transferring co-owner. After this period, he is given formal notice to respond and, if he remains silent for fifteen days, his declaration of pre-emption is null and void by operation of law, without prejudice to damages that may be claimed by the transferor.

When the transferor has granted payment terms and, as a result of economic circumstances, the value of the property that has fallen to him has increased or decreased by more than one quarter since the partition, the sums remaining due increase or decrease in the same proportion, unless this variation is excluded by the parties.

###### Article 935

When a creditor seizes all or part of the rights of a co-owner in the joint ownership with a view to subjecting them to a forced sale, there is no right of pre-emption but a right of substitution for the successful bidder. The lawyer of the pursuing creditor or the notary notifies all the other co-owners one month before the scheduled date of the sale. The latter have a period of one month from the adjudication, to substitute themselves for the purchaser.
This right is exercised by declaration at the registry of the Court of First Instance or with the notary in charge of the sale. It is recorded in the schedule of conditions of sale established for the sale.

###### Article 936

For both amicable and forced transfers, compliance with notification and time limit rules is required on pain of nullity of the transaction. This nullity, of private interest, is available for five years to the persons

to whom the notifications should have been made or to their heirs.

The notifications provided for by the two articles and the preceding paragraph must be addressed to every bare owner and to every usufructuary. But a usufructuary may acquire a share in bare ownership only if no bare owner comes forward as purchaser; a bare owner may acquire a share in usufruct only if no usufructuary comes forward as purchaser.

###### § 2. Rules for management of co-ownership Article 937

In co-ownership, decisions are made unanimously, subject to the following exceptions.

###### Article 938

When they fall within the normal operation of co-owned property, decisions concerning the following may be made by the holders of two-thirds of the co-ownership rights:
1° Acts of administration of co-owned property;
2° The designation of a co-owner or a third party under a general management mandate;
3° The conclusion and renewal of leases other than those relating to property for agricultural, commercial, industrial or artisanal use;
4° The decision to sell movable co-owned property when this transaction is necessary for payment of the debts and charges of the co-ownership. The sale of co-owned property outside this purpose requires unanimity, except by judicial authorization.

###### Article 939

Except in case of division of ownership of the property or if one of the co-owners is in one of the cases provided for in Article 863, the alienation of co-owned property may be authorized by the Court of First Instance, at the request of one or more co-owners holding at least two-thirds of the co-ownership rights, according to the conditions and procedures defined in the following paragraphs.
The co-owner or co-owners holding at least two-thirds of the co-ownership rights express before a notary, by this majority, their intention to proceed with the alienation of the co-owned property. Within the month that follows, the notary has this intention served on the other co-owners.
In the absence of opposition within three months of service, the decision to alienate the co-owned property is confirmed, unless the service provided for in the second paragraph has not been effected. In case of opposition, the Court of First Instance may authorize the alienation of the co-owned property if it does not cause excessive harm to the rights of the other co-owners.

This alienation is effected by licitation. The sums derived therefrom may not be reinvested except to pay the debts and charges of the co-ownership.

###### Article 940

Any co-owner may take the measures necessary for the preservation of co-owned property, even if there is no urgency.
These conservatory acts may be of a material nature, such as an act of occasional maintenance, or legal, such as formal notice to a debtor in default. They may be directed both against another co-owner and against a third party to the co-ownership.

The co-owner may use for this purpose the co-ownership funds held by him and he is deemed to have free disposal thereof with regard to third parties.
