When one of the debtors becomes the sole heir of the creditor, or when the creditor becomes the sole heir of one of the debtors, the confusion extinguishes the joint and several claim only for the part and portion of the debtor or the creditor.

###### Article 1499

The creditor who consents to the division of the debt with respect to one of the co-debtors retains his joint and several action against the others, but subject to deduction of the share of the debtor whom he has released from joint and several liability.

###### Article 1500

The creditor who receives separately the share of one of the debtors, without reserving in the receipt joint and several liability or his rights in general, renounces joint and several liability only with respect to that debtor.
The creditor is not deemed to remit joint and several liability to the debtor when he receives from him a sum equal to the portion for which he is liable, if the receipt does not state that it is for his share.
The same applies to a simple demand made against one of the co-debtors for his share, if the latter has not acquiesced to the demand, or if a judgment of condemnation has not intervened.

###### Article 1501

The creditor who receives separately and without reservation the portion of one of the co-debtors in the arrears or interest of the debt, loses joint and several liability only for the arrears or interest due, and not for those to become due, nor for the principal, unless the divided payment has been continued for ten consecutive years.

###### Article 1502

Between themselves, joint and several co-debtors contribute to the debt each only for his share.

The one who has paid beyond his share has recourse against the others in proportion to their own share.
If one of them is insolvent, his share is distributed, by contribution, among the solvent co-debtors, including the one who made the payment and the one who benefited from a remission of joint and several liability.
On the other hand, if the debt proceeds from a matter that concerns only one of the joint and several co-debtors, the latter alone is liable for the debt with respect to the others; if he has paid it, he has no recourse against his co-debtors; if they have paid it, they have recourse against him.

###### Article 1503

Joint and several co-debtors are jointly and severally liable for non-performance of the obligation. The burden ultimately falls on those to whom the non-performance is attributable.

###### § 2. Divisible and indivisible obligations Article 1504

An obligation is divisible or indivisible according to whether its object is either a thing which in its delivery, or an act which in its performance, is or is not susceptible of division, whether material or intellectual.

###### Article 1505

An obligation is indivisible, even though the thing or act which is its object is divisible by its nature, if the aspect under which it is considered in the obligation does not render it susceptible of partial performance.

###### Article 1506

Each of the creditors of an indivisible obligation, whether by nature or by contract, may demand and receive full payment thereof, subject to accounting to the others; but he may not alone dispose of the claim or receive the price in lieu of the thing.

Each of the debtors of such an obligation is bound for the whole; but he has recourse for contribution against the others.
The same applies to each of the successors of these creditors and debtors.

#### Chapitre II

Transactions in obligations Section I: Assignment of claims

###### Article 1507

Assignment of a claim is a contract by which the assigning creditor transfers, for valuable consideration or gratuitously, all or part of his claim against the assigned debtor to a third party called the assignee.
It may relate to one or more claims, present or future, determined or determinable. It extends to the accessories of the claim.
The consent of the debtor is not required, unless the claim has been stipulated as non-assignable.

###### Article 1508

Assignment of a claim must be evidenced in writing, on pain of nullity.

###### Article 1509

As between the parties, the transfer of the claim takes effect on the date of the instrument.

It is enforceable against third parties from that moment. In case of dispute, proof of the date of the assignment lies with the assignee, who may provide it by any means.
However, the transfer of a future claim takes place only on the day it comes into existence, both as between the parties and with respect to third parties.

###### Article 1510

The assignment is not enforceable against the debtor, if he has not already consented thereto, unless it has been notified to him or he has acknowledged it.
The debtor may raise against the assignee defences inherent in the debt, such as payment, prescription, nullity, exception of non-performance, termination or set-off of related debts. He may also raise defences arising from his relations with the assignor before the assignment became enforceable against him, such as the granting of a time period, remission of debt or set-off of unrelated debts.

The assignor and the assignee are jointly and severally liable for all additional costs occasioned by the assignment which the debtor need not advance. Unless otherwise stipulated, the burden of these costs falls on the assignee.

###### Article 1511

Competition between successive assignees of a claim is resolved in favour of the first in time; he has recourse against the person to whom the debtor has made payment.
The date to be taken into consideration is that of each of the assignments, proof of which may be provided by any means.

###### Article 1512

A person who assigns a claim for valuable consideration warrants the existence of the claim and its accessories, unless the assignee has acquired it at his own risk or was aware of the uncertain nature of the claim.
He is liable for the solvency of the debtor only when he has undertaken to be so, and up to the amount of the price he has obtained from the assignment of his claim. Any clause to the contrary is deemed unwritten.

Where the assignor has warranted the solvency of the debtor, this warranty is understood only as to present solvency; it may however extend to solvency at maturity, but on condition that the assignor has expressly specified it.

##### Section II: Novation Article 1513

Novation is a contract the object of which is to substitute for an obligation, which it extinguishes, a new obligation which it creates.
It may take place by substitution of obligation between the same parties, by change of debtor or by change of creditor.

###### Article 1514

Novation is not presumed; the intention to effect it must clearly result from the instrument.

###### Article 1515

Novation takes place only if the old obligation and the new obligation are both valid, unless its declared object is to substitute a valid undertaking for an undertaking tainted with a defect.

###### Article 1516

Novation by change of debtor may be effected without the participation of the first debtor.

###### Article 1517

Novation by change of creditor requires the consent of the debtor. The latter may, in advance, accept that the new creditor be designated by the first.
The novation is enforceable against third parties on the date of the instrument. In case of dispute as to the date of the novation, proof thereof lies with the new creditor, who may provide it by any means.

###### Article 1518

Novation by substitution of obligation between the same parties is possible, whatever the difference established between the old and the new obligation.

###### Article 1519

The extinction of the old obligation extends to all its accessories.

By way of exception, original security interests may be reserved for the guarantee of the new obligation with the consent of third-party guarantors.

###### Article 1520

Novation agreed between the creditor and one of the joint and several co-debtors releases the others.

Novation agreed between the creditor and a surety does not release the principal debtor. It releases the other sureties up to the contributory share of the one whose obligation has been the subject of the novation.

##### Section III: Delegation Article 1521

Delegation is a transaction by which a person, the delegator, obtains from another, the delegatee, that he expressly bind himself towards a third party, the delegated creditor, who accepts him as debtor.
The delegatee may not, unless otherwise stipulated, raise against the delegated creditor any defence derived from his relations with the delegator or from the relations between the latter and the delegated creditor.

###### Article 1522

Where the delegator is debtor of the delegated creditor and the intention of the delegated creditor to discharge the delegator expressly results from the instrument, the delegation operates novation.
However, the delegator remains liable if he has expressly undertaken to warrant the future solvency of the delegatee or if the latter is subject to debt settlement proceedings at the time of the delegation.

###### Article 1523

Where the delegator is debtor of the delegated creditor but the latter has not discharged him from his debt, the delegation gives the delegated creditor a second debtor.
Payment made by one of the two debtors releases the other, to the corresponding extent.

###### Article 1524

Where the delegator is creditor of the delegatee, his claim is extinguished only by performance of the delegatee's obligation towards the delegated creditor and to the corresponding extent.
Until then, the delegator may demand or receive payment thereof only for the part that would exceed the delegatee's undertaking. He recovers his rights only by performing his own obligation towards the delegated creditor.

Assignment or seizure of the delegator's claim produces effect only subject to the same limitations.

However, if the delegated creditor has released the delegator, the delegatee is himself released with respect to the delegator, up to the amount of his undertaking towards the delegated creditor.

###### Article 1525

The simple indication made by the debtor of a person designated to pay in his place does not entail novation or delegation. The same applies to the simple indication made, by the creditor, of a person designated to receive payment for him.

#### Chapter III: Actions Available to the Creditor Article 1526

The creditor has the right to performance of the obligation; he may compel the debtor to perform under the conditions provided by law and especially by the provisions of the code of civil procedure.

###### Article 1527

When the debtor's failure to exercise his rights and actions of a patrimonial nature compromises the rights of his creditor, the latter may, by oblique action, exercise them on behalf of his debtor,

with the exception of those which are exclusively attached to his person. Rights exclusively attached to the person of the debtor are rights and actions whose exercise is subject to personal considerations of a moral or family nature.

###### Article 1528

The creditor may also act in his own name, by way of the Paulian action, to have acts done by his debtor in fraud of his rights declared unenforceable against him, provided he establishes, in the case of an act for valuable consideration, that the third party co-contractor had knowledge of the fraud.
The action is available when the debtor has performed an act of impoverishment aimed at organizing his insolvency or making the creditor's enforcement more difficult. It is also available when the creditor has a special right over property of the debtor and the latter performs an act which has the effect of impairing that special right.

The claim must be certain on the day the action is brought. The enforceability and liquidity of the claim are not conditions for the Paulian action.

###### Article 1529

In cases determined by law, the creditor may act directly for payment of his claim against a debtor of his debtor.

#### Chapter IV

Extinction of the Obligation Section I: Payment

###### Subsection 1: General Provisions

###### Article 1530

Payment is the voluntary performance of the obligation due.

It must be made as soon as the debt becomes enforceable; it may be made even by a person who is not obligated to do so, except in case of legitimate refusal by the creditor.
Payment releases the debtor towards the creditor and extinguishes the debt, except when the law or the contract provides for subrogation in the rights of the creditor.

###### Article 1531

Payment must be made to the creditor or to the person designated to receive it.

Payment made to a person who was not qualified to receive it is nevertheless valid if the creditor ratifies it or if he has benefited from it.
Payment made to a creditor lacking capacity to contract is not valid, unless he has benefited from it.

###### Article 1532

Payment made in good faith to an apparent creditor is valid.

###### Article 1533

The creditor may refuse partial payment even if the performance is divisible. He may agree to receive in payment something other than what is owed to him.

###### Article 1534

The debtor of an obligation to deliver a specific thing is released by its delivery to the creditor in its condition, except to prove, in case of deterioration, that it is not due to his act or to that of persons for whom he must answer.

If the debt is of a thing which is determined only by its kind, the debtor shall not be required, in order to be released, to give it of the best kind; but he may not offer it of the worst kind.

###### Article 1535

In the absence of another designation by law, contract or judge, payment must be made at the domicile of the debtor.

###### Article 1536

The costs of payment are, except where otherwise provided by law or clause, borne by the debtor.

###### Article 1537

Payment is proved by any means.

###### Article 1538

The voluntary delivery by the creditor to the debtor of the original under private signature or of the enforceable copy of the title of his claim constitutes a simple presumption of release.
The same delivery to one of the joint and several co-debtors produces the same effect towards all.

###### Article 1539

The debtor of several debts may indicate, when he pays, which one he intends to discharge.

In the absence of indication by the debtor, imputation takes place as follows: first on debts that have fallen due; among these, on debts which the debtor had the greatest interest in discharging. Where interests are equal, imputation is made on the oldest; all things being equal, it is made proportionally.

###### Subsection 2: Special Provisions for Obligations of Sums of Money

###### Article 1540

The debtor of an obligation of a sum of money is released by payment of its nominal amount. The amount of the sum due may however vary through indexation or debts of value.
A debt of value is an obligation which has as its object, not a determined sum of money, but a value which may give rise, according to the times, to different estimates, such as the debt of reparation which is determined on the day of judgment and not on the day of the harmful act. The debtor of a debt of value is released by payment of the sum of money resulting from its liquidation.

###### Article 1541

When the obligation of a sum of money bears interest, the debtor is released by paying the principal and the interest. Partial payment is imputed first to interest, except by contrary agreement.
Interest is granted by law or stipulated in the contract. The rate of contractual interest must be fixed in writing. It is deemed annual by default.

###### Article 1542

Interest that has fallen due, owed for at least one full year, produces interest if the contract has so provided or if a judicial decision so specifies.

###### Article 1543

Payment, in Djibouti, of an obligation of a sum of money is made in Djibouti Francs. However, payment may take place in another currency if the obligation so denominated proceeds from an international contract or from a foreign judgment.

###### Article 1544

In the absence of another designation by law, contract or judge, the place of payment of the obligation of a sum of money is the domicile of the creditor.

###### Article 1545

The judge may, taking into account the situation of the debtor and in consideration of the needs of the creditor, postpone or schedule, within the limit of two years, the payment of sums due.
By special and reasoned decision, he may order that the sums corresponding to postponed instalments shall bear interest at a reduced rate at least equal to the legal rate, or that payments shall be imputed first to the capital.

He may make these measures subject to the performance by the debtor of acts designed to facilitate or guarantee payment of the debt.
The judge's decision suspends enforcement proceedings that would have been initiated by the creditor. Increases in interest or penalties provided for in case of delay are not incurred during the period fixed by the judge.

Any contrary stipulation is deemed unwritten.
The provisions of this article are not applicable to maintenance debts.

###### Subsection 3: Notice to Perform

###### Article 1546

Notice to perform is the act by which either the creditor clearly indicates to his debtor that he does not intend to allow a contractual non-performance to continue, or the debtor enjoins his creditor not to obstruct performance of the contract.

###### § 1. Notice to Perform to the Debtor Article 1547

The debtor is given notice to pay either by a summons or an act containing sufficient demand, or, if the contract so provides, by the mere enforceability of the obligation.

###### Article 1548

Notice to perform to pay an obligation of a sum of money starts the running of default interest, at the legal rate. The creditor does not have to justify prejudice.

###### Article 1549

Notice to perform to deliver a thing places the risks on the debtor, if they are not already there.

###### § 2

Formal notice to the creditor or "tender of payment" Article 1550
Where the creditor, at maturity and without legitimate reason, refuses to receive the payment due to him or prevents it by his act, the debtor may give him formal notice to accept it or to permit its performance. This formal notice constitutes a tender of payment.
Formal notice to the creditor stops the running of interest owed by the debtor and places the risks of the thing on the creditor, if they are not already there. It is otherwise in case of gross or fraudulent fault of the debtor.

Formal notice does not interrupt prescription.

###### Article 1551

If the obstruction has not ended within two months of the formal notice, the debtor may, where the obligation relates to a sum of money, deposit it with the registry of the Court of First Instance or, where the obligation relates to the delivery of a thing, sequester it with a professional custodian.
If sequestration of the thing is impossible or too costly, the judge may authorize its private sale or sale by public auction. After deduction of the costs of the sale, the price is deposited with the registry of the Court of First Instance.

Deposit or sequestration releases the debtor from the time of their notification to the creditor.

###### Article 1552

Where the obligation relates to another object, for example an obligation to do, the debtor is released if the obstruction has not ceased within two months of the formal notice.

###### Article 1553

The costs of formal notice and of deposit or sequestration are borne by the creditor.

###### Sub-section 4: Payment with subrogation

###### Article 1554

Subrogation takes place by operation of law alone for the benefit of one who, having a legitimate interest, makes payment provided that his payment releases, towards the creditor, the person who is bound by the final burden of all or part of the debt.

###### Article 1555

Conventional subrogation is effected at the initiative of the creditor when the latter, receiving his payment from a third person, subrogates him in his rights against the debtor.
This subrogation must be express.

It must be granted at the same time as the payment, unless, in a prior act, the subrogor has manifested the intention that his contracting party be subrogated to him upon payment. The concomitance of subrogation and payment may be proved by any means.

###### Article 1556

Subrogation also takes place when the debtor, borrowing a sum for the purpose of paying his debt, subrogates the lender in the rights of the creditor with the latter's concurrence. In this case, the subrogation must be express and the receipt given by the creditor must indicate the origin of the funds.
Subrogation may be granted without the concurrence of the creditor, but on condition that the debt is due or that the term is in favor of the debtor. It is then necessary that the loan agreement and the receipt be executed before a notary, that in the loan agreement it be declared that the sum has been borrowed to make the payment, and that in the receipt it be declared that the payment has been made from the sums paid for that purpose by the new creditor.

###### Article 1557

Subrogation cannot harm the creditor when he has been paid only in part; in this case, he may exercise his rights, for what remains due to him, in preference to the person from whom he has received only partial payment.
Subrogation transfers to its beneficiary, within the limit of what he has paid, the claim and its accessories, with the exception of rights exclusively attached to the person of the creditor.

However, the subrogee is entitled only to legal interest from the time of formal notice, if he has not agreed with the debtor on a new interest. These interests are guaranteed by the security interests attached to the claim, within the limits, where they have been created by third parties, of their initial commitments if they do not consent to be bound beyond.

###### Article 1558

The debtor may invoke subrogation as soon as he has knowledge of it but it may be set up against him only if it has been notified to him or if he has acknowledged it.
Subrogation is enforceable against third parties from the time of payment.
The debtor may set up against the subrogated creditor defenses inherent in the debt, such as nullity, exception of non-performance, termination or set-off of related debts. He may also set up against him defenses arising from his relations with the subrogor before the subrogation became enforceable against him, such as the granting of a term, remission of debt or set-off of unrelated debts.

##### Section II: Set-off

###### Sub-section 1: General rules Article 1559

Set-off is the simultaneous extinction of reciprocal obligations between two persons.

It takes effect, subject to being invoked, to the extent applicable, on the date when its conditions are met.

###### Article 1560

Subject to the provisions set out in the following sub-section, set-off takes place only between two fungible, certain, liquidated and due obligations.
Fungible are obligations of sums of money, even in different currencies, provided they are convertible, or those which have as their object a quantity of things of the same kind.

###### Article 1561

Unseizable claims and obligations to return a deposit, a loan for use or a thing of which the owner has been unjustly deprived are subject to set-off only if the creditor consents thereto.

###### Article 1562

A grace period does not prevent set-off.

###### Article 1563

If there are several debts subject to set-off, the rules of imputation of payments in articles 1392, 1394 and 1398 are transposable.

###### Article 1564

The debtor who has acknowledged without reservation the assignment of the claim may not set up against the assignee the set-off that he could have set up against the assignor.

###### Article 1565

The surety may set up against the creditor the set-off that occurred between the latter and the principal debtor.

The joint and several co-debtor may avail himself of the set-off that occurred between the creditor and one of his co-obligors to have the divisible share of the latter deducted from the total debt.

###### Article 1566

Set-off does not prejudice rights acquired by third parties.

###### Sub-section 2: Special rules Article 1567

Set-off may be pronounced in court even if one of the obligations, although certain, is not yet liquidated or due. Unless otherwise decided, set-off then produces its effects on the date of the decision.

###### Article 1568

The judge may not refuse set-off of related debts on the sole ground that one of the obligations is not liquidated or due.
In this case, set-off is deemed to have occurred on the day of the maturity of the first of them.
In the same case, the acquisition of rights by a third party over one of the obligations does not prevent its debtor from setting up set-off.

###### Article 1569

The parties may freely agree to extinguish all reciprocal obligations, present or future, by set-off; this takes effect on the date of their agreement or, in the case of future obligations, on that of their coexistence.

##### Section III: Merger Article 1570

Merger results from the union of the capacities of creditor and debtor of the same obligation in the same person. It extinguishes the claim and its accessories, subject to rights acquired by or against third parties.

###### Article 1571

Where there is solidarity between several debtors or between several creditors, and the confusion concerns only one of them, the extinction takes place, with regard to the others, only for his share.
Where the confusion concerns a guaranteed obligation, the surety, even if solidary, is released. Where the confusion concerns the obligation of one of the sureties, the principal debtor is not released. The other solidary sureties are released up to the amount of that surety's share.

##### Section IV : La remise de dette Article 1572

Release from debt is the contract by which the creditor releases the debtor from his obligation.

###### Article 1573

Release from debt granted to one of the solidary co-debtors releases the others up to the amount of his share.

Release from debt made by only one of the solidary creditors releases the debtor only for the share of that creditor.

###### Article 1574

Release from debt granted to the principal debtor releases the sureties, even if solidary.

Release granted to one of the solidary sureties does not release the principal debtor, but releases the others up to the amount of his share.

What the creditor has received from a surety for the discharge of his suretyship must be credited against the debt and discharge the principal debtor proportionally. The other sureties remain liable only after deduction of the share of the released surety or of the value provided if it exceeds that share.

##### Section V : L'impossibilité d'exécuter Article 1575

Impossibility of performing the prestation releases the debtor to the appropriate extent where it proceeds from a case of force majeure and it is definitive, unless he has agreed to take responsibility for it or he has been previously placed in default.

###### Article 1576

Where the impossibility of performance results from the loss of the thing due, the debtor placed in default is nevertheless released if he proves that the loss would have occurred similarly if the obligation had been performed. He is however bound to transfer to his creditor the rights and actions attached to the thing.

#### Chapitre V : Les restitutions

###### Article 1577

Restitution of a thing other than a sum of money takes place in kind or, where that is impossible, in value, estimated on the day of restitution.

###### Article 1578

The person who restores the thing is liable for degradations and deteriorations which have diminished its value, unless he is in good faith and they are not due to his fault.

###### Article 1579

The person who having received the thing in good faith has sold it, must restore only the sale price.

If he received it in bad faith, he owes its value on the day of restitution where it is greater than the price.

###### Article 1580

Restitution includes the fruits and the value of the enjoyment that the thing has provided. The value of the enjoyment is assessed by the judge on the day he rules.
Unless otherwise stipulated, restitution of the fruits, if they are not found in kind, takes place according to a value estimated on the date of reimbursement, according to the state of the thing on the day of payment of the obligation.

###### Article 1581

Restitutions due to an unemancipated minor or to a protected adult are reduced in proportion to the profit he has derived from the annulled act.

###### Article 1582

To fix the amount of restitutions, account is taken to the person who must restore, even if he is in bad faith, of the necessary and useful expenses for the preservation of the thing, within the limit of the increased value estimated on the day of restitution.

###### Article 1583

Restitution of a sum of money includes interest at the legal rate and taxes paid into the hands of the person who received it.

###### Article 1584

The person who has received in bad faith owes the interest, the fruits he has received or the value of the enjoyment from the time of payment. The person who has received in good faith owes them only from the day of the demand.

###### Article 1585

Restitution of a service has lieu in value. This is assessed on the date on which it was provided.
Securities constituted for payment of the obligation are transferred by operation of law to the obligation to restore without however depriving the surety of the benefit of the term.

### Titre V : De la preuve civile

###### Article 1586

The burden of proof lies on the person who claims recognition of a right or performance of an obligation.
Reciprocally, the person who claims to be released must justify the fact which produced the extinction of the right asserted against him.

Judicial administration of proof and disputes relating thereto are governed by the code of civil procedure.

Chapitre Ier : L'admissibilité des modes de preuve Article 1587
Except in cases where the law provides otherwise, proof may be provided by any means.

###### Article 1588

A juridical act relating to a sum or value exceeding the sum or value of 100,000 FD, must be proved by writing under private signature or authentic.
It cannot be proved beyond or against a writing establishing a juridical act, even if the sum or value does not exceed that amount, except by another writing under private signature or authentic.
The person whose claim exceeds the threshold mentioned in the first paragraph cannot be exempted from proof by writing by restricting his demand.

The same applies to the person whose demand, even if less than that amount, relates to the balance or to part of a claim greater than that amount.

###### Article 1589

The rules provided for in Article 1588 are subject to exception:
-	in case of material or moral impossibility of obtaining a writing,
-	if it is customary not to establish a writing,
-	or where the writing has been lost as a result of an external cause.

###### Article 1590

Writing may also be supplemented by judicial admission, the decisive oath or a commencement of proof by writing corroborated by another means of proof.

###### Article 1591

A commencement of proof by writing constitutes any written act which emanated from the person against whom the demand is made, or from the person he represents, and which makes the alleged fact plausible.
Declarations made by a party during his personal appearance, his refusal to answer or his absence from the appearance may be considered by the judge as equivalent to a commencement of proof by writing.

The mention of an authentic or private signature writing in a public register is equivalent to a commencement of proof by writing.

#### Chapitre II : La preuve par écrit

##### Section I : Dispositions générales

###### Article 1592

No one may constitute a title for himself.

###### Article 1593

Proof of a juridical act may be preconstituted by a writing in authentic form or under private signature.
Where a party does not know how to read, write or sign, if it is a question of an authentic act, the public officer shall have the fingerprints of that person affixed on the act after having read it to him and asked whether he consents to it. If it is a question of an act under private signature, the person who does not know how to read, write or sign, first chooses a person of his choice who reads the act to him, then affixes his fingerprint on the said act, finally the chosen person signs the act as witness.

###### Article 1594

Writing consists of a sequence of letters, characters, numbers or any other signs or symbols endowed with an intelligible meaning, whatever their medium.

###### Article 1595

Electronic writing has the same probative force as writing on paper medium, provided that the person from whom it emanates can be duly identified and that it is established and preserved in conditions likely to guarantee its integrity.

###### Article 1596

The signature necessary for the perfection of a legal act identifies its author. It manifests their consent to the obligations arising from that act. When it is affixed by a public officer, it confers authenticity on the act.
When it is electronic, it consists in the use of a reliable identification process guaranteeing its link with the act to which it is attached.

###### Article 1597

In the absence of contrary provisions or agreements, the judge resolves conflicts of written evidence by determining by any means the most credible instrument.

##### Section II: The Authentic Act Article 1598

An authentic act is one that has been received, with the required formalities, by a public officer having the right to execute instruments in the place where the act was drawn up.

###### Article 1599

An act that is not authentic due to the incompetence or incapacity of the officer, or due to a defect in form, is valid as a privately signed writing if it has been signed by the parties.

###### Article 1600

An authentic act is evidence until impugnment for forgery of what the public officer states to have personally accomplished or observed.
Nevertheless, in case of complaints of principal forgery, the execution of the act alleged to be forged shall be suspended by the indictment; and, in case of impugnment for forgery made incidentally, the courts may, depending on the circumstances, provisionally suspend the execution of the act.

##### Section III: The Privately Signed Act

###### Article 1601

A privately signed act, acknowledged by the party against whom it is invoked or legally deemed acknowledged with respect to that party, is evidence between those who executed it and with respect to their heirs and successors in title.

###### Article 1602

A person against whom a privately signed act is invoked is obliged to formally acknowledge or disavow their handwriting or signature.
Their heirs or successors in title may similarly disavow the handwriting or signature of their predecessor, or may simply declare that they do not recognize the handwriting or signature of their predecessor. In these cases, verification of handwriting is ordered by the court.

###### Article 1603

A privately signed act that records a synallagmatic contract is evidence only if it has been made in as many originals as there are parties having a distinct interest, unless the parties have agreed to entrust to a third party the sole copy drawn up.
One original is sufficient for all persons having the same interest.

Each original must contain mention of the number of originals that have been made.

A party who has performed the contract, even partially, may not invoke the lack of plurality of originals or of mention of their number.
The requirement of a plurality of originals is deemed satisfied for contracts in electronic form when the act is established and preserved in accordance with Articles 1595 and second paragraph of 1596, and the process allows each party to have a copy on a durable medium or to have access to it.

###### Article 1604

A privately signed act by which one party alone undertakes towards another to pay them a sum of money or to deliver a fungible good must include the signature of the person who subscribes to this undertaking as well as the mention, written by that person, of the sum or quantity in words and figures.
If the party declares that they do not know how or cannot sign, express mention is made in the act of their declaration, as well as of the reason preventing them from signing. The act bears their fingerprint.

###### Article 1605

When the sum expressed in the body of the act differs from that expressed by the handwritten mention, the privately signed act is evidence for the sum written in words.

###### Article 1606

A privately signed act acquires certain date with respect to third parties only from the day it was registered, the day of death of a signatory, or the day its substance is recorded in an authentic act.

##### Section IV: Other Writings Article 1607

Registers and documents that professionals must keep or establish have, against their author, the same probative force as privately signed writings; but a person relying on them may not divide the entries to retain only those that are favorable to them.

###### Article 1608

Domestic registers and papers do not constitute evidence in favor of the person who wrote them. They constitute evidence against that person:
1° In all cases where they formally state a payment received;
2° When they contain express mention that the writing was made to remedy the lack of an instrument in favor of the person for whom they state an obligation.

###### Article 1609

The mention of a payment or other cause of discharge entered by the creditor on an original instrument that has always remained in their possession constitutes a simple presumption of discharge of the debtor.
The same applies to a mention entered on the duplicate of an instrument or a receipt, provided that this duplicate is in the hands of the debtor.

##### Section V: Copies of Instruments Article 1610

Copies, when the original instrument subsists, are evidence only of what is contained in the instrument, the presentation of which may always be required.
When the original instrument no longer exists, a reliable copy has the same probative force as the original. Reliability is left to the judge's assessment. Nevertheless, an executory or authentic copy of an authentic writing is deemed reliable; the same applies to copies that have been made by authority of the magistrate, with parties present or duly summoned, or to those that have been made in the presence of the parties and with their mutual consent.

Copies that the judge does not consider reliable may serve only as a commencement of proof in writing.
Copies of copies may, depending on the circumstances, be considered as mere information.

###### Article 1611

The transcription of an act in public registers may serve only as a commencement of proof in writing; for this it will even be necessary:
1° That it be established that all the minutes of the notary, for the year in which the act appears to have been made, are lost, or that proof be given that the loss of the minute of this act occurred through a particular accident;
2° That there exist a proper repertory of the notary, which establishes that the act was made on the same date.
When, by means of the concurrence of these two circumstances, proof by witnesses is admitted, it will be necessary that those who were witnesses to the act, if they still exist, be heard.

##### Section VI: Recognitive Acts Article 1612

A recognitive act is a legal act that records the existence of a prior act without modifying its substance. It constitutes acknowledgment of the pre-existing obligation. A recognitive act does not dispense with presentation of the original instrument, unless its content is specifically recited therein.

What it contains that is additional or different from the original instrument has, in the absence of express intent to novate, no effect.

Nevertheless, if there were several conforming acknowledgments, supported by possession, and one of which is thirty years old, the creditor may be dispensed from producing the original instrument.

#### Chapter III: Proof by Witnesses Article 1613

The probative value of statements made by a third party under the conditions of the code of civil procedure is left to the judge's assessment.

#### Chapter IV: Presumptions Article 1614

Presumptions are consequences that the law or the magistrate draws from a known fact to an unknown fact.

##### Section I: Legal Presumptions Article 1615

A legal presumption is one which is attached by law to certain acts or certain facts, and which holds them to be certain.

It dispenses the person for whose benefit it exists from providing proof thereof or shifts the object of proof.

The presumption is said to be simple when the law reserves proof to the contrary; it is said to be irrefragable when it cannot be overturned.

###### Article 1616

The authority of res judicata applies only with regard to what was the subject of the judgment. It is necessary that the thing claimed be the same; that the claim be based on the same cause; that the claim be between the same parties, and brought by them and against them in the same capacity.

###### Article 1617

Agreements on proof are valid when they relate to rights over which the parties have free disposal.
Nevertheless, they cannot contradict irrefragable presumptions established by law, nor modify the faith attached to admission or oath. Nor can they establish an irrefragable presumption for the benefit of one of the parties.

##### Section II: Judicial Presumptions Article 1618

Judicial presumptions are not established by law, but are left to the assessment of the judge, who must admit them only if they are serious, precise and concordant, and only in cases where the law admits proof by any means.

#### Chapter V: Admission by a Party

###### Article 1619

Admission is the declaration by which a person acknowledges as true a fact of a nature to produce legal consequences against them.
The admission that is opposed to a party is either extrajudicial or judicial.

###### Article 1620

Purely verbal extrajudicial admission is received only in cases where the law permits proof by any means.
Its probative value is left to the assessment of the judge.

###### Article 1621

Judicial admission is the declaration made in court by the party or their specially mandated representative. It has full faith against the person who made it.
It cannot be divided against its author.
It cannot be revoked, unless it is proved that it was the result of an error of fact; it could not be revoked on the pretext of an error of law.

#### Chapter VI: The Oath Article 1622

The judicial oath is of two kinds:
1° That which one party refers to the other to make the judgment of the case depend on it: it is called decisory.
2° That which is referred ex officio by the judge to one or the other of the parties.

##### Section I: The Decisory Oath Article 1623

The decisory oath may be referred on any kind of dispute whatsoever.

###### Article 1624

It can be referred only on a fact personal to the party to whom it is referred.

###### Article 1625

It may be referred at any stage of the case, and even when there exists no beginning of proof of the claim or exception on which it is invoked.

###### Article 1626

The oath may be referred back to the person who refers it, except when the fact which is its object is not that of both parties, but is purely personal to the person to whom the oath had been referred.

###### Article 1627

The person to whom the oath is referred, who refuses it or does not consent to refer it back to their adversary, or the adversary to whom it has been referred back and who refuses it, must fail in their claim or exception.

###### Article 1628

The oath constitutes proof only for the benefit of the person who referred it and their heirs and successors in title, or against them.

The oath referred by one of the joint and several creditors to the debtor releases the latter only for the share of that creditor.
The oath referred to the principal debtor also releases the sureties. That referred to one of the joint and several debtors benefits the co-debtors.
That referred to the surety benefits the principal debtor.
In these last two cases, the oath of the joint and several co-debtor or of the surety benefits the other co-debtors or the principal debtor only when it has been referred on the debt, and not on the fact of joint and several liability or suretyship.

##### Section II: The Oath Referred Ex Officio Article 1629

The judge may refer to one of the parties the oath, either to make the decision of the case depend on it, or only to determine the amount of the condemnation.

###### Article 1630

The judge cannot refer the oath ex officio, either on the claim or on the exception opposed to it, except under the following two conditions; it is necessary:
1.	That the claim or exception not be fully justified;
2.	That it not be totally devoid of proof.
Outside these two cases, the judge must either grant or purely and simply reject the claim.

###### Article 1631

The oath referred ex officio by the judge to one of the parties cannot be referred back by that party to the other.

###### Article 1632

The oath on the value of the thing claimed can be referred by the judge to the claimant only when it is otherwise impossible to establish that value.
The judge must even, in that case, determine the sum up to which the claimant will be believed on their oath.

### Title VI: Marriage Contract and Matrimonial Property Regimes

Chapter I. General Provisions Article 1633
The law governs the conjugal association, as to property, only in the absence of special agreements, which the spouses may make as they see fit, provided that they are not contrary either to good morals or to the provisions that follow.

###### Article 1634

The spouses, in the marriage certificate, indicate whether or not they have entered into a marriage contract.

They declare whether they opt for the matrimonial property regime of the civil code. Mention thereof is made in the marriage certificate.

When they opt for the regime of the civil code, they indicate the matrimonial property regime they choose. In the absence of stipulations in this regard, the spouses shall be subject to the regime of legal community (

###### article 1647

et seq.); and, with regard to third parties, the spouses shall be deemed married under this regime of common law each time they seize the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance or accept its jurisdiction when they are in defense, unless in the acts entered into with those third parties, they have declared having made a marriage contract falling under such regime as they have indicated to them.

###### Article 1635

The spouses cannot derogate from either the duties or the rights that result for them from marriage or that are provided by law under the title of parental authority and guardianship.

###### Article 1636

The spouses cannot make any agreement or waiver the object of which would be to change the legal order of successions, without prejudice to inter vivos or testamentary gifts that may take place according to the forms and in the cases determined by this code.

###### Article 1637

The spouses can no longer stipulate in a general manner that their association will be governed by one of the customs, laws or local statutes that could govern the various parts of the Djiboutian territory, and which are repealed by this code.

###### Article 1638

All matrimonial agreements shall be drafted, before the marriage, by notarial deed, in the presence and with the simultaneous consent of the future spouses and all persons who are parties thereto or their agents. Matrimonial agreements take effect on the day of the celebration of the marriage and cannot receive any change after that celebration.
Changes or counter-letters that could be made to these agreements before the celebration of the marriage must be recorded by deed executed before a notary and the presence and simultaneous consent of all persons who were parties thereto.

###### Article 1639

The notary shall issue to the parties, at the time of signing the contract, a certificate on plain paper and free of charge, stating his or her names and place of residence, the names, first names, capacities and residences of the future spouses, as well as the date of the contract. This certificate indicates that it must be given to the civil registrar before the celebration of the marriage, which the notary also reminds the future spouses of orally.
In case of changes made to the initial deed, the notary shall draft them following the original of the marriage contract; the notary may not issue either engrossments or copies of the marriage contract without transcribing following them the changes or counter-letters that may have been made to it. In the absence of compliance with these formalities, the changes or counter-letters shall have no effect with regard to third parties.

###### Article 1640

A minor capable of contracting marriage may consent to all the agreements of which this contract is susceptible; and the agreements and donations that he or she has made therein are valid, provided that he or she has been assisted, in the contract, by the persons whose consent is necessary for the validity of the marriage.
An adult under guardianship or curatorship may enter into matrimonial agreements if he or she is assisted, in the contract, by his or her guardian or curator.
If matrimonial agreements have been entered into without this assistance, annulment may be requested by the incapable person or by the persons whose consent was required, but only for one year from the marriage.

###### Article 1641

Once the marriage has been celebrated, no change may be made to the matrimonial regime except by effect of a judgment:

1° When one of the spouses requests judicial separation of property by reason of disorder in the affairs or misconduct of the spouse endangering his or her interests;
2° When partial and temporary modifications to the rules setting the powers of the spouses are granted by the judge, such as when the other spouse is unable to express his or her will and judicial authorization to act without the consent of the other spouse is granted (

###### article 225

of this code), or when judicial authorization to represent the other spouse has been decided (

###### article 227

of this code), or in the case of transfer of powers over ordinary or reserved community property (

###### article 1671

of this code), or transfer of powers over separate property (

###### article 1674 of this code)

3° By effect of a notarial deed, if necessary approved by the judge, in the case of article 1642.

###### Article 1642

After two years of application of the matrimonial regime, the spouses may agree, in the interest of the family, to modify it, or even to change it entirely, by a notarial deed. Mention of the modification is made on the original of the modified marriage contract and, on pain of nullity, the notarial deed contains the liquidation of the modified matrimonial regime if it is necessary.
The persons who had been parties to the modified contract and the adult children of each spouse are personally informed of the proposed modification; the creditors of the spouses are informed of it by publication of a notice in a newspaper authorized to receive legal announcements. Each of them may oppose the modification within a period of three months.

In case of opposition, the notarial deed is submitted to the approval of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance of the domicile of the spouses. It is compulsorily so when either spouse has minor children. The application and the decision of approval are published.

Non-opposing creditors, if their rights have been defrauded, may challenge the change of matrimonial regime to have this deed declared unenforceable against them, subject to establishing, if it is an onerous transaction, that the third party co-contractor had knowledge of the fraud. They must specify how the contested fraudulent acts are related to the change of matrimonial regime, which is not in itself indicative of fraud

###### Article 1643

The change of matrimonial regime takes effect between the parties on the date of the deed or judgment providing for it and, with regard to third parties, three months after mention has been made of it in the margin of the marriage certificate. However, even in the absence of this mention, the change is nonetheless enforceable against third parties if, in deeds entered into with them, the spouses have declared that they have modified their matrimonial regime.
When either spouse is subject to a legal protection measure under the conditions provided for in Title XII of Book I of this code, the change or modification of the matrimonial regime is subject to prior authorization from the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance or the family council if one has been constituted.

By exception, agreements entered into by spouses in divorce proceedings with a view to liquidating their matrimonial regime fall under the provisions provided for by this code specific to the divorce proceedings initiated.

###### Article 1644

When a change to the matrimonial regime occurs by application of a foreign law governing the effects of the union, the spouses inform the persons who had been parties to the marriage contract and each of their adult children and proceed, if necessary, with land registration. They have mention of it made in the margin of the marriage certificate.

###### Article 1645

The change of matrimonial regime takes effect between the parties from the date of the decision or deed providing for it and, with regard to third parties, three months after the publicity formalities provided for in article 1644 have been completed.

However, in the absence of completion of these formalities, the change of matrimonial regime is enforceable against third parties if, in deeds entered into with them, the spouses have declared that they have modified their matrimonial regime.

#### Chapter II: Of the community regime Article 1646

The community, whether legal or conventional, begins on the day of the marriage contracted before the civil registrar: it cannot be stipulated that it will begin at another time.

##### Section I: Of the legal community Article 1647

The community that is established in the absence of a contract, or by the simple declaration that one is marrying under the community regime, is subject to the rules explained in the subsections that follow.

###### Subsection 1: Of what composes the community actively and passively

###### § 1. Of the assets of the community Article 1648

The community is composed actively of acquisitions made by the spouses together or separately during the marriage, and coming both from their personal industry and from savings made on the fruits and income of their separate property.

###### Article 1649

Any property, movable or immovable, is presumed to be a community acquisition if it is not proved that it is separate property of one of the spouses by application of a provision of the law. If the property is of those that do not bear in themselves proof or mark of their origin, the personal ownership of the spouse, if contested, must be established in writing. In the absence of an inventory or other pre-constituted proof, the judge may take into consideration all writings, including family titles, registers and domestic papers, as well as bank documents and invoices. He or she may even admit proof by testimony or presumption, if he or she finds that a spouse was in a material or moral impossibility of obtaining a writing.

###### Article 1650

Each spouse retains full ownership of his or her separate property. The community is entitled only to fruits collected and not consumed. But compensation may be due to it, upon dissolution of the community, for fruits that the spouse has neglected to collect or has fraudulently consumed, without any inquiry, however, being admissible beyond the last five years.

###### Article 1651

Property that is separate by nature, even if acquired during the marriage, includes clothing and linen for the personal use of one of the spouses, actions for compensation for bodily or moral injury, inalienable claims and pensions, and, more generally, all property that has a personal character and all rights exclusively attached to the person. Also separate by nature, but subject to compensation if applicable, are the work instruments necessary for the profession of one of the spouses, unless they are an accessory to a business or operation forming part of the community.

###### Article 1652

Property remains separate if the spouses had ownership or possession of it on the day of the celebration of the marriage, or if they acquire it, during the marriage, by succession, donation or legacy. The liberality may stipulate that the property that is its object shall belong to the community. Property falls into the community, unless otherwise stipulated, when the liberality is made to both spouses jointly. Property abandoned or transferred by father, mother or other ascendant to one of the spouses, either to fulfill what is owed to him or her, or subject to paying the donor's debts to third parties, remains separate, subject to compensation.

###### Article 1653

Property acquired as accessories to separate property as well as new securities and other increases relating to separate movable securities form separate property, subject to compensation if applicable. Also separate property, by the effect of real subrogation, are claims and indemnities that replace separate property, as well as property acquired by employment or reinvestment, in accordance with articles 1678 and 1679.

###### Article 1654

Property acquired in exchange for property that belonged separately to one of the spouses is itself separate, subject to compensation due to or by the community, if there is a balancing payment. However, if the balancing payment charged to the community exceeds the value of the property transferred, the property acquired in exchange falls into the common mass, subject to compensation in favor of the transferor.

###### Article 1655

The acquisition made, by auction or otherwise, of a portion of property of which one of the spouses was an undivided owner, does not form an acquisition, subject to compensation due to the community for the sum it may have provided.

###### § 2.Du passif de la communauté Article 1656

The community is composed passively:
-	on a definitive basis, of maintenance owed by the spouses and debts contracted by them for the upkeep of the household and the education of the children, in accordance with article 228;
-	on a definitive basis or subject to compensation, depending on the case, of other debts arising during the community.

###### Article 1657

Debts for which the spouses were liable on the day of the celebration of their marriage, or with which the successions and liberalities that fall to them during the marriage are burdened, remain personal to them, both in principal and in arrears or interest.

###### Article 1658

The creditors of one or the other spouse, in the case of article 1657, may pursue their payment only against the separate property and income of their debtor.
They may, nevertheless, also seize the property of the community when the movable property that belongs to their debtor on the day of the marriage or that has fallen to him or her by succession or liberality has been merged into the common patrimony and can no longer be identified according to the rules of article 1649.

###### Article 1659

Compensation is due to the community that has discharged the personal debt of a spouse.

###### Article 1660

Payment of debts for which each spouse is liable, for whatever cause, during the community, may always be pursued against the common property, unless there has been fraud by the debtor spouse and bad faith by the creditor, subject to compensation due to the community if applicable.

###### Article 1661

The earnings and wages of a spouse may be seized by the creditors of his or her spouse only if the obligation was contracted for the upkeep of the household or the education of the children, in accordance with article 228.

###### Article 1662

Each of the spouses may only bind his or her separate property and income, by a guarantee or a loan, unless these have been contracted with the express consent of the other spouse who, in that case, does not bind his or her separate property.

###### Article 1663

The community that has discharged a debt for which it could be pursued under the preceding articles is nevertheless entitled to compensation, whenever that commitment had been contracted in the personal interest of one of the spouses, such as for the acquisition, preservation or improvement of separate property.

###### Article 1664

The community is entitled to compensation, after deduction, if applicable, of the profit derived by it, when it has paid fines incurred by a spouse, by reason of criminal offenses, or the damages and costs to which he or she had been sentenced for civil delicts or quasi-delicts. It is likewise entitled to compensation if the debt it has discharged had been contracted by one of the spouses in disregard of the duties imposed on him or her by marriage.

###### Article 1665

When a debt has entered the community on behalf of only one of the spouses, it may not be pursued against the separate property of the other. If there is joint and several liability, the debt is deemed to enter the community on behalf of both spouses.

###### Sous-section 2 : De l'administration de la communauté et des biens propres Article 1666

Each of the spouses has the power to administer the common property alone and to dispose of it, subject to being liable for faults he or she may have committed in his or her management. Acts accomplished without fraud by one spouse are binding on the other. The spouse who exercises a separate profession alone has the power to accomplish the acts of administration and disposition necessary for it. All subject to articles 1667 to 1670.

###### Article 1667

The spouses may not, one without the other, dispose inter vivos, gratuitously, of community property. Nor may they, one without the other, assign one of these properties as security for the debt of a third party.

###### Article 1668

The legacy made by a spouse may not exceed his or her share in the community. If a spouse has bequeathed an item of the community, the legatee may claim it in kind only insofar as the item, by the event of the

partition, falls into the lot of the testator's heirs; if the item does not fall into the lot of these heirs, the legatee has compensation for the total value of the bequeathed item, against the share, in the community, of the heirs of the testator spouse and against the personal property of the latter.

###### Article 1669

The spouses may not, one without the other, alienate or encumber with real rights the immovable property, businesses and operations belonging to the community, nor the non-negotiable partnership rights and corporeal movables whose alienation is subject to publicity. They may not, without their spouse, collect the capital proceeds from such operations. Likewise, they may not, one without the other, transfer community property into a fiduciary patrimony.

###### Article 1670

The spouses may not, one without the other, lease a rural property or an immovable property for commercial, industrial or artisanal use belonging to the community. Other leases on common property may be entered into by one spouse alone and are subject to the rules provided for leases entered into by the usufructuary.

###### Article 1671

If one of the spouses is, in a lasting manner, unable to express his or her will, or if his or her management of the community demonstrates unfitness or fraud, the other spouse may apply to the court to be substituted in the exercise of his or her powers. The provisions of Articles 1689 to 1692 are applicable to this application.
The spouse, thus authorized by the court, has the same powers as the spouse he or she replaces would have had; he or she performs with judicial authorization the acts for which his or her consent would have been required if there had been no substitution. The spouse deprived of his or her powers may, subsequently, apply to the court for their restitution, by establishing that their transfer to the other spouse is no longer justified.

###### Article 1672

If one of the spouses has exceeded his or her powers over the common property, the other, unless he or she has ratified the act, may apply for its annulment. The action for nullity is open to the spouse for two years from the day on which he or she became aware of the act, without ever being able to be brought more than two years after the dissolution of the community.

###### Article 1673

Each spouse has the administration and enjoyment of his or her separate property and may dispose of it freely.

###### Article 1674

If one of the spouses is, in a lasting manner, unable to express his or her will, or if he or she endangers the interests of the family, either by allowing his or her separate property to deteriorate, or by dissipating or misappropriating the income derived therefrom, he or she may, at the request of his or her spouse, be divested of the rights of administration and enjoyment recognized to him or her by Article 1673. The provisions of Articles 1689 to 1691 are applicable to this application.
Unless the appointment of a judicial administrator appears necessary, the judgment confers upon the applicant spouse the power to administer the separate property of the divested spouse, as well as to collect the fruits thereof, which must be applied by him or her to the charges of the marriage and the surplus used for the benefit of the community. From the date of the application, the divested spouse may dispose alone only of the bare ownership of his or her property. He or she may, subsequently, apply to the court to be restored to his or her rights, if he or she establishes that the causes which had justified the divestment no longer exist.

###### Article 1675

If, during the marriage, one of the spouses entrusts the other with the administration of his or her separate property, the rules of mandate are applicable. The mandatary spouse is, however, dispensed from accounting for the fruits, when the power of attorney does not expressly require it.

###### Article 1676

When one of the spouses takes over the management of the separate property of the other, with the latter's knowledge, and nevertheless without opposition on his or her part, he or she is deemed to have received a tacit mandate, covering acts of administration and enjoyment, but not acts of disposition. This spouse is liable for his or her management to the other as a mandatary. He or she is, however, accountable only for existing fruits; for those which he or she has neglected to collect or fraudulently consumed, he or she may be pursued only within the limit of the last five years.
If it is in defiance of a recorded opposition that one of the spouses has interfered in the management of the separate property of the other, he or she is liable for all the consequences of his or her interference and accountable without limitation for all the fruits which he or she has collected, neglected to collect or consumed.

###### Article 1677

The community owes compensation to the owner spouse whenever it has derived profit from separate property. This is the case, in particular, when it has received separate funds or funds from the sale of separate property, without employment or reinvestment having been made.
If a dispute is raised, proof that the community has derived profit from separate property may be provided by all means, even by testimony and presumptions.

###### Article 1678

Employment or reinvestment is deemed to have been made with respect to a spouse whenever, at the time of an acquisition, he or she has declared that it was made with separate funds or funds from the alienation of separate property, and to serve as employment or reinvestment for him or her. In the absence of this declaration in the act, employment or reinvestment takes place only by agreement of the spouses, and it produces its effects only in their mutual relations.

###### Article 1679

If employment or reinvestment is made in anticipation, the property acquired is separate, on condition that the sums expected from the separate patrimony are paid to the community within five years from the date of the act.

###### Article 1680

When the price and costs of the acquisition exceed the sum for which employment or reinvestment has been made, the community is entitled to compensation for the excess.
If, however, the contribution of the community is greater than that of the acquiring spouse, the property acquired falls into the community, subject to the compensation due to the spouse.

###### Article 1681

Whenever a sum is taken from the community, either to discharge debts or charges personal to one of the spouses, such as the price or part of the price of property separate to him or her or the redemption of feudal services, or for the recovery, preservation or improvement of his or her personal property, and generally whenever one of the two spouses has derived a personal profit from the property of the community, he or she owes compensation therefor.

###### Article 1682

If the father and mother have jointly endowed the common child without expressing the portion in which they intended to contribute thereto, they are deemed to have endowed each for one half, whether the dowry was provided or promised in property of the community, or whether it was provided in property personal to one of the two spouses. In the second case, the spouse whose personal property was constituted as dowry has, against the property of the other, an

action for indemnity for half of said dowry, having regard to the value of the property given at the time of the endowment.

###### Article 1683

The dowry constituted to the common child, in property of the community, is chargeable to the latter. It must be borne for one half by each spouse, upon the dissolution of the community, unless one of them, in constituting it, has expressly declared that he or she would assume responsibility for the whole or for a share greater than one half.

###### Article 1684

The guarantee of the dowry is owed by any person who has constituted it; and its interest runs from the day of the marriage, even though there is a term for payment, if there is no stipulation to the contrary.

###### Sous-section 3 : De la dissolution de la communauté

###### § 1. Des causes de dissolution et de la séparation de biens Article 1685

The community is dissolved:
1° by the death of one of the spouses; 2° by declared absence;
3° by divorce;
4° by legal separation; 5° by separation of property;
6° by change of matrimonial regime.

###### Article 1686

There can be no continuation of the community, notwithstanding any stipulations to the contrary.

The spouses may, either one, request, if appropriate, that, in their mutual relations, the effect of the dissolution be carried back to the date when they ceased to cohabit and collaborate.

###### Article 1687

If, by the disorder of the affairs of a spouse, his or her bad administration or his or her misconduct, it appears that the maintenance of the community endangers the interests of the other spouse, the latter may pursue separation of property in court. Any separation, without the intervention of the judge, is null and void.

###### Article 1688

Separation of property, although pronounced by the court, is null if the proceedings tending to liquidate the rights of the parties have not been commenced within three months of the judgment having become final and if the final settlement has not occurred within one year of the opening of the liquidation operations.
This period of one year may be extended by the President of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance ruling in summary proceedings.

###### Article 1689

The application and the judgment of separation of property must be published under the conditions and subject to the penalties provided for by the Code of Civil Procedure.
The judgment pronouncing the separation of property takes effect, as to its effects, from the day of the application.

Mention of the judgment shall be made in the margin of the marriage certificate as well as on the original of the marriage contract.

###### Article 1690

The creditors of a spouse may not request separation of property on his or her behalf.

###### Article 1691

When an action for separation of property has been initiated, creditors may summon the spouses by lawyer-to-lawyer notice to communicate to them the application and supporting documents. They may even intervene in the proceedings to preserve their rights.
If the separation was pronounced in fraud of their rights, they may challenge it by third-party opposition, under the conditions provided for in the Code of Civil Procedure.

###### Article 1692

The spouse who has obtained separation of property must contribute, in proportion to his or her means and those of his or her spouse, both to household expenses and to the costs of educating the children. He or she must bear these costs entirely if nothing remains to the other.

###### Article 1693

Separation of property pronounced by court has the effect of placing the spouses under the regime of Articles 1739 et seq. The court, in pronouncing the separation, may order that one spouse pay his or her contribution to his or her spouse, who shall henceforth assume alone with respect to third parties the settlement of all marriage charges.

###### Article 1694

Agreements entered into pursuant to Article 293 are suspended, as to their effects, until the divorce is pronounced; they may not be executed, even in relations between spouses, until the judgment has become final. Either spouse may request that the divorce judgment modify the agreement if the consequences of the divorce fixed by that judgment call into question the basis of the liquidation and partition.

###### § 2. De la liquidation et du partage de la communauté Article 1695

Once the community is dissolved, each spouse takes back those assets that had not entered the community, if they exist in kind, or the assets that have been subrogated thereto. Liquidation of the common mass, assets and liabilities, must then take place.

###### Article 1696

An account is established in the name of each spouse of the compensation owed by the community to him or her and the compensation he or she owes to the community, according to the rules prescribed in the preceding sections.

###### Article 1697

Compensation is, in general, equal to the lesser of the two sums represented by the expenditure made and the profit remaining. It may not, however, be less than the expenditure made when the latter was necessary. It may not be less than the profit remaining when the borrowed value was used to acquire, preserve or improve an asset that is found, on the day of liquidation of the community, in the borrowing estate. If the asset acquired, preserved or improved was alienated before liquidation, the profit is valued on the day of alienation; if a new asset has been subrogated to the alienated asset, the profit is valued on that new asset.

###### Article 1698

If, on balance, the account shows a balance in favor of the community, the spouse returns the amount to the common mass. If it shows a balance in favor of the spouse, the latter has the choice either to demand payment or to withdraw common assets up to the amount due.

###### Article 1699

Withdrawals are made first from cash, then from movables, and subsidiarily from immovables of the community. The spouse making the withdrawal has the right to choose the movables and immovables he or she will withdraw. He or she may not, however, prejudice by his or her choice the rights that his or her spouse may have to request maintenance of the indivision or preferential attribution of certain assets. If the spouses wish to withdraw the same asset, the matter is resolved, except for demonstration of abuse by the one who opposes the withdrawal of a specific asset by the other, by drawing lots.

###### Article 1700

In case of insufficiency of the community, the withdrawals of each spouse are proportional to the amount of compensation owed to him or her. However, if the insufficiency of the community is attributable to the fault of one of the spouses, the other spouse may exercise his or her withdrawals before the former on all common assets; he or she may exercise them subsidiarily on the separate assets of the responsible spouse.

###### Article 1701

Compensation owed by the community or to the community bears interest by operation of law from the day of dissolution. However, when the compensation is equal to the profit remaining, interest runs from the day of liquidation.

###### Article 1702

Withdrawals from common assets constitute a partition transaction. They confer on the spouse exercising them no right to be preferred over creditors of the community.

###### Article 1703

After all withdrawals have been made from the mass, the surplus is divided in half between the spouses. If an immovable of the community is an annex to another immovable belonging separately to one of the spouses, or if it is contiguous to that immovable, the spouse owner has the option of having it attributed to him or her by imputation on his or her share or in exchange for an equalizing payment, according to the value of the asset on the day the attribution is requested.

###### Article 1704

The partition of the community, with respect to all matters concerning its forms, the maintenance of indivision and preferential attribution, the sale by auction of assets, the effects of partition, the warranty and equalizing payments, is subject to all the rules established in the title On Successions for partitions among co-heirs.
However, for communities dissolved by divorce, legal separation or separation of property, preferential attribution is never automatic, and it may always be decided that the totality of any equalizing payment due shall be payable in cash.

###### Article 1705

The spouse who has misappropriated or concealed any effects of the community is deprived of his or her share in said effects. Likewise, the spouse who has knowingly concealed the existence of a common debt must assume it definitively.

###### Article 1706

After partition is completed, if one of the two spouses is a personal creditor of the other, as when the price of his or her asset was used to pay a personal debt of his or her spouse, or for any other cause, he or she exercises his or her claim on the share that fell to the latter in the community or on his or her personal assets.

###### Article 1707
